text:
Company Description

About SNV

SNV is a global development partner, deeply rooted in the countries where we operate. We are driven by a vision of a better world: A world where across every society all people live with dignity and have equitable opportunities to thrive sustainably.

To make this vision a reality, we need transformations in vital agri-food, energy, and water systems. SNV contributes by strengthening capacities and catalysing partnerships in these sectors. We help strengthen institutions and effective governance, reduce gender inequalities and barriers to social inclusion, and enable adaptation and mitigation to the climate and biodiversity crises.

Building on 60 years of experience, we support our partners with our technical and process expertise and methodological rigor. We do this in more than 20 countries in Africa and Asia with a team of approximately 1,600 colleagues. By being adaptable and tailoring our approaches to these different contexts, we can contribute to impact at scale, resulting in more equitable lives for all.

SNV has been working in Vietnam since 1995 and currently has over 70 national and international experts. SNV Vietnam implements projects in more than 30 provinces across the country, including the poorest and most remote areas.

About the Study

The aviation sector faces an acute decarbonisation challenge. Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is widely recognised as the most viable near-term pathway to reducing aviation emissions at scale, yet its global scale-up is constrained by the availability of reliable, cost-competitive, and sustainably sourced feedstocks. Rice residue (straw and husks left after harvest) produced in vast quantities across the Mekong Delta of Vietnam represents one of the most promising and underexplored feedstock opportunities in Southeast Asia.

SNV Vietnam is undertaking a Comprehensive Rice-to-SAF Value Chain Feasibility Study to assess the technical, economic, environmental, and operational feasibility of mobilising rice residues at scale in Vietnam for use as SAF feedstock. The study covers 3-4 Mekong Delta provinces (including An Giang, Đồng Tháp, and Long An) and addresses five core research questions:

RQ1: Current Use & Value Mapping - how rice straw and husks are currently used and the financial/agronomic incentives required to redirect them into the SAF supply chain.

RQ2: Aggregation Bottleneck Assessment - localised logistical, financial, and infrastructure constraints to large-scale residue extraction.

RQ3: Pricing & High-Integrity Benchmarks - delivered price ranges along the supply chain, benchmarked against ICAO/CORSIA standards.

RQ4: Environmental Risk Analysis - soil health, safe extraction thresholds, and GHG modelling vs. the open-burning baseline (ICAO/CORSIA aligned).

RQ5: Offtake Feasibility & Supply Modelling - Monte Carlo simulations of supply reliability, regulatory framework review, and contract precedent analysis.

The study will draw on a substantial body of existing data and evidence alongside additional primary data collection determined necessary during the study design phase. It will also convene a formal Advisory Group (international and national members) and incorporate structured government engagement. Final outputs include a comprehensive study report, executive summary, statistical analyses, data visualisations, and Advisory Group outputs, delivered by March 2027.

SNV Vietnam is now seeking a consultant to serve as the Research and Data Lead, acting as the principal technical counterpart to the Study Manager, providing methodological leadership on survey design, enumerator training, data collection quality assurance, and statistical analysis — including the Monte Carlo supply reliability modelling that anchors the study's investment-grade evidence base.

Job Description

Objectives and Scope of Work

The Research and Data Lead will serve as the principal technical counterpart to the Study Manager and the lead in-country methodological resource for the Comprehensive Rice-to-SAF Value Chain Feasibility Study. The Research and Data Lead focuses on the technical and analytical rigour of the study, ensuring survey instruments, sampling frameworks, enumerator preparation, data quality protocols, and statistical analyses all meet the standards required for a study of this ambition.

The Research and Data Lead will work closely with the Team Lead, the SNV Global MEL Advisor, the Study Manager, other Study team members, contracted survey firms, and academic partners to carry out the following activities:

Survey design and instrument development: With guidance from the Team Leader, design and iterative refinement of all quantitative and qualitative data collection instruments — including farm household surveys, aggregator/SME questionnaires, key informant interview (KII) guides, and focus group discussion (FGD) protocols. Ensure instruments are methodologically rigorous, aligned to the study's five research questions, calibrated to Vietnamese context, and structured to enable robust downstream statistical analysis (including Monte Carlo modelling).

Sampling framework design: In partnership with the Team Lead and Global MEL Advisor, design the multi-stage stratified sampling framework for the study, including power calculations, stratification logic, and province-level allocation targets across the 3-4 target Mekong Delta provinces. Document all sampling assumptions and provide the analytical basis for scaling or adjusting samples during fieldwork.

Enumerator training and technical preparation: Design and co-deliver the technical components of enumerator training — including instrument familiarisation, survey programming/scripting, use of digital data collection platforms (e.g., ODK, KoBoToolbox, SurveyCTO), interview technique, data quality checks. Work alongside the Study Manager for selecting and contracting the survey firm and managing the logistical relationship with the contracted survey firm, to ensure enumerators are technically prepared to deliver the study to specification.

Data quality assurance during fieldwork: Serve as the principal technical monitor of data quality across the fieldwork period. Design and operate real-time data quality dashboards, review incoming data for logic errors, anomalies, and enumerator drift, flag issues for resolution with the contracted survey firm, and resolve issues with the contracted survey firm in a timely manner. Conduct spot-check field visits as required to verify data collection integrity.

Statistical analysis and modelling: Lead the statistical analysis of all primary and secondary data, including descriptive analysis, cross-tabulations, price and cost curve modelling, and inferential analysis where appropriate. Design and execute the Monte Carlo simulation of supply reliability under climate, seasonal, and offtake scenarios (RQ5), calibrating input distributions against primary survey data (farm-level yields, seasonal variations, competing uses, and aggregator capacity).

Data harmonisation and visualisation: Lead data cleaning, harmonisation across sources (primary survey data, secondary datasets, GIS layers), and the production of analytical visualisations for the study report, executive summary, and Advisory Group outputs. Ensure all analytical outputs are transparent, reproducible, and clearly documented.

Technical inputs to reporting: Contribute technical inputs to the inception report, preliminary analysis memo, comprehensive study report, and executive summary — with particular responsibility for the methodological, sampling, statistical, and Monte Carlo modelling sections. Ensure that analytical claims are appropriately caveated and that confidence ranges are transparently presented.

MEL framework support: Working under the direction of the Team Lead and Global MEL Advisor, contribute to the design and quality assurance of the overall MEL framework for the study, including analysis plans, data management protocols, and quality assurance procedures.

The Research and Data Lead will provide an estimated level of effort of up to 50 working days over the 7-month assignment period, from September 2026 to 31 March 2027. The role is Vietnam-based, with work taking place primarily in the Mekong Delta provinces (An Giang, Đồng Tháp, Long An) aligned with enumerator training, fieldwork monitoring, and validation activities.

Due Diligence Instructions

Due Diligence (DD) checks apply to individual consultants engaged by SNV for the provision of consultancy services. Conducting these checks supports SNV in managing donor funds responsibly, ethically, and in full compliance with relevant regulations. To apply, download the Microsoft Word Due Diligence and Vetting Form, click https://c.smartrecruiters.com/sr-company-attachments-prod-aws-dc5/58919688e4b0672cc03331a9/aad96d4c-3d4c-478e-8cc0-03bc9ed8e135?r=s3-eu-central-1

Qualifications

Eligibility and Qualifications

The assignment is open to individual Vietnamese national consultants who meet the following criteria:

Vietnamese national with permanent residence in Vietnam (required).

Advanced postgraduate degree (Master's required; PhD desirable) in a discipline relevant to survey research and quantitative analysis, such as statistics, biostatistics, econometrics, applied economics, agricultural / environmental / behavioural economics, quantitative research methods, or a related field.

Minimum of 5 years' senior-level experience in the design and technical delivery of primary data collection and quantitative analysis for feasibility, market, or applied research studies in Vietnam, with substantive experience serving as the principal methodological and analytical lead on multi-source, multi-province studies.

Demonstrated experience designing survey instruments, sampling frameworks (including power calculations), enumerator training curricula, and data quality assurance protocols for large-scale primary data collection.

Strong methodological grounding in mixed-methods research design and MEL frameworks, including sampling frameworks, quantitative and qualitative data collection instruments, complex statistical analysis, interpretation, and reporting, and data quality assurance protocols.

Demonstrated experience conducting advanced statistical analyses, including at least one of: probabilistic modelling (Monte Carlo simulation or equivalent), scenario or sensitivity analysis, econometric modelling, or supply reliability modelling.

Substantive technical familiarity with at least one of the following areas relevant to the study: rice systems and rice residue / straw management; low-emission agricultural value chains; biomass, bioenergy, or sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) feedstocks; agri-food supply chain analysis; or climate finance and carbon markets in Vietnamese agriculture.

Working familiarity with recognised international sustainability and carbon accounting frameworks relevant to low-emission agriculture and SAF feedstocks (e.g., ICAO/CORSIA, Gold Standard, or comparable standards) is desirable.

Prior experience in the Mekong Delta is strongly preferred, particularly in An Giang, Đồng Tháp, and Long An provinces.

Strong analytical, writing, and editorial skills, including the ability to translate technical statistical outputs into decision-ready analytical narratives with clearly caveated claims and transparent confidence ranges (sample analytical products may be required).

Advanced proficiency in statistical software such as Stata, R, or Python, and in survey platforms (e.g., ODK, KoBoToolbox, SurveyCTO), as well as MS Office (Word, Excel, PowerPoint).

Excellent command of English (written and spoken) is required to work effectively with the International Team Lead and international co-investment partners.

text:
American Airlines’ recent milestone in collaboration with clean fuels company Infinium puts the spotlight on eSAF, the even-cleaner version of SAF (sustainable aviation fuel). This is eSAF produced locally in Texas, and currently seen as the best option for real reductions in CO2 emissions associated with commercial aviation.

A recent American Airlines flight from Corpus Christi International Airport (CRP) to Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) marked an important moment not just for the airline, but for commercial aviation in the US. That’s because it demonstrated the real-world feasibility of something called eSAF, a type of ultra-low carbon electrofuel.

eSAF is not the same as SAF, which is made from different types of bio-based feedstock. eSAF is obtained using waste CO2 and green electricity. Both are drop-in fuels for aircraft, which need to be blended with conventional jet fuel in specific proportions in order to be certified (based on ASTM International’s specification for JetA) for safe use in today’s aircraft engines.

The eSAF for this milestone flight came from Infinium, a clean fuels company operating what is considered the world’s first drop-in eFuels facility. This facility is called Pathfinder, it’s located in Corpus Christi, Texas, and it became operational in 2023. It produces eFuels using renewable electricity from wind and solar resources available in the region, plus waste CO2 provided by Howard Energy Partners, located right next to Project Pathfinder.

This wasn’t just the first real-world deployment of Infinium’s eSAF, but also the first delivery of SAF made without bio-based feedstock to a commercial airport in the US. The eSAF was produced at the Pathfinder facility, blended with commercial jet fuel, then delivered to the existing, standard fueling infrastructure at CRP for the American Airlines passenger flight to DFW.

American Airlines and Infinium have already signed an offtake agreement for commercial volumes of eSAF. This clean jet fuel won’t come from the Pathfinder facility, but from a future facility, Project Roadrunner, located in West Texas. Project Roadrunner will turn an existing gas-to-liquid facility into a clean fuel facility. It will use wind and solar assets purposely-built for its operations, and captured emissions from different operators in the area.

This innovative project is already under construction and set to kick off production and deliveries in 2027, with a planned output of more than 5 million gallons of eSAF annually.

eSAF is only one of Infinium’s clean products, along with eDiesel (for medium and heavy-duty trucks), and eNaphtha (a replacement for petroleum-derived napahtha used in the chemical and industrial sectors, including plastics and solvents production). Infinium’s eSAF for aviation is an ultra-low carbon, energy-dense fuel that can reduce lifecycle GHG emissions by more than 90% compared to fossil-based jet fuel.

title: Why are airlines keeping older aircraft in service for longer? - Aerospace Global News
description:
Why are aircraft delivery delays forcing airlines to keep older fleets?
Older aircraft are less efficient than the latest generation models, but they are still essential during a period of strong travel demand and limited capacity.
For airlines, keeping older aircraft flying has become a necessity rather than a choice.
How long will airlines keep older aircraft in service?
Until aircraft availability improves, airlines will continue relying on older fleets to maintain operations.
text:
What started as a post-pandemic production slowdown has turned into a much bigger challenge for the aviation industry.

Airbus and Boeing are still facing delivery delays, while manufacturers and suppliers continue to deal with shortages of parts, skilled workers and the production capacity needed to build aircraft at the pace airlines need.

Here we dive deeper into why airlines are always looking to (safely) extend aircraft life wherever possible.

Why are aircraft delivery delays forcing airlines to keep older fleets?

Aircraft deliveries remain below the levels required to meet airline demand, leaving thousands of aircraft on order but unavailable for operators.

For airlines, waiting for new aircraft is no longer measured in months; in many cases, it is taking years.

As a result, carriers are changing their fleet strategies. Rather than retiring older aircraft when replacements arrive, many are investing in additional maintenance, cabin upgrades and refurbishment programmes to keep existing fleets flying safely.

New aircraft remain the preferred option because they offer better fuel efficiency, lower maintenance costs and improved passenger experience. However, delayed deliveries have left airlines with limited alternatives.

How are supply chain problems affecting aircraft production?

The shortage of new aircraft also reflects wider disruption across the aviation supply chain. Earlier this year, we reported on A350 delays due to Spirit AeroSystems supply issues as just one example.

Aircraft production depends on thousands of suppliers providing components including engines, avionics and advanced materials. Shortages of parts, workforce challenges and manufacturing bottlenecks have slowed production across the industry.

Engine availability has also become a significant issue, with some airlines facing longer maintenance turnaround times and reduced aircraft availability.

How are airlines keeping aging aircraft in service?

Older aircraft are less efficient than the latest generation models, but they are still essential during a period of strong travel demand and limited capacity.

Airlines are extending aircraft lifespans through heavy maintenance checks, structural inspections, cabin modernisation and technology upgrades. Aircraft that were once expected to leave fleets are now remaining in service for several additional years.

However, ageing fleets come with higher maintenance costs, more reliance on spare parts and increased fuel consumption compared with newer aircraft.

For airlines, keeping older aircraft flying has become a necessity rather than a choice.

What impact is this having on airline operations and growth?

Aircraft shortages are affecting airline plans worldwide. Some carriers have delayed new routes, reduced flight frequencies or postponed expansion because additional aircraft have not arrived as expected.

The limited availability of aircraft has also increased leasing costs, as airlines compete for capacity from a smaller pool of available planes.

For passengers, this can mean fewer schedule options. For airlines, it means managing rising demand with fewer resources.

How do older aircraft affect aviation’s net zero targets?

The biggest concern surrounding delayed aircraft deliveries is their impact on aviation’s climate ambitions.

New generation aircraft are much more fuel-efficient. By keeping ageing fleets in service longer, airlines are delaying some of the emissions reductions expected from fleet renewal.

Fleet replacement remains one of aviation’s most important tools for reducing carbon emissions. Alongside sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), operational improvements and future technologies, newer aircraft are expected to play a key role in achieving net zero emissions by 2050.

How long will airlines keep older aircraft in service?

The aviation industry is already working to increase SAF production, improve efficiency and develop future technologies. However, without enough new aircraft entering service, reducing emissions becomes more difficult.

Airlines are not abandoning their sustainability goals; they are managing a situation where one of the most effective short-term solutions – that is, replacing older aircraft – is being delayed.

Manufacturers are working to increase production, but supply chain pressures are expected to continue for the foreseeable future. Until aircraft availability improves, airlines will continue relying on older fleets to maintain operations.

Extending aircraft lifespans is helping the industry manage today’s challenges, but it’s something of a sticking plaster solution to a much larger problem.

title: Jetstar and Qatar Airways Jets Narrowly Avoid Collision at Sydney Airport as Safety Concerns Mount
description:
Key Highlights Jetstar-Qatar near-miss: A Jetstar A320 carrying about 180 passengers was forced to brake suddenly after coming dangerously close to a Qatar Airways Boeing 777 being towed at Sydney Airport.
The incident occurred at about 7am as the Jetstar aircraft, carrying around 180 passengers and bound for the Gold Coast, was taxiing for departure.
Footage recorded inside the Jetstar aircraft captured the pilot explaining the situation to passengers after the aircraft stopped.
Air traffic restrictions add to the concern The near-collision occurred against a backdrop of operational difficulties at Sydney Airport.
At the same time, Sydney Airport remains one of Australia's most intensively used aviation facilities.
text:
Key Highlights

Jetstar-Qatar near-miss: A Jetstar A320 carrying about 180 passengers was forced to brake suddenly after coming dangerously close to a Qatar Airways Boeing 777 being towed at Sydney Airport.

Crew member injured: The abrupt stop injured a Jetstar cabin crew member. No passengers were reported injured.

Conflicting accounts: The Jetstar pilot indicated that instructions may not have been followed by the Qatar aircraft and ground crew, while Jetstar maintains its pilots were following Air Traffic Control instructions. An investigation will establish what happened.

Second major runway incident in weeks: The near-miss comes shortly after a July 27 incident in which a Qantas 737 was cleared to cross a runway while a QantasLink Q400 was landing. The ATSB described that incident as a “breakdown of co-ordination.”

Growing scrutiny of Sydney operations: With recent disruptions, ATC restrictions and previous runway-safety incidents, investigators will examine communications, clearances, staffing, procedures and recorded data to determine whether wider operational issues contributed to the latest near-miss.

A Jetstar Airbus A320 and a Qatar Airways Boeing 777 came dangerously close to colliding on the ground at Sydney Airport on Sunday morning, in the latest of a series of aviation safety incidents to raise questions about coordination and air traffic control operations at Australia's busiest airport.

The incident occurred at about 7am as the Jetstar aircraft, carrying around 180 passengers and bound for the Gold Coast, was taxiing for departure. The Qatar Airways Boeing 777 was empty and being towed when the two aircraft came into close proximity.

The Jetstar pilots were forced to apply the brakes suddenly, bringing the A320 to an abrupt stop only metres from the much larger Qatar aircraft. A Jetstar cabin crew member was injured in the sudden braking. No passengers were reported injured.

Footage recorded inside the Jetstar aircraft captured the pilot explaining the situation to passengers after the aircraft stopped.

“With the sudden stop we have had a situation where one of our cabin crew has been injured,” the pilot said, before indicating that the aircraft would return to the bay.

The pilot also appeared to raise concerns about what had happened on the ground, saying the crew had been instructed to hold short while they concentrated on crossing a runway. He said the other aircraft and ground crew had, according to the information available to him, not followed instructions.

However, the cause of the incident has not been established.

Jetstar said its pilots were following Air Traffic Control instructions when they were forced to brake.

“Our aircraft was following instructions by Air Traffic Control when the pilots were forced to brake firmly after another aircraft came in close proximity,” a Jetstar spokesman said.

“We have commenced an investigation into the incident.”

That distinction is important. While the cockpit account has raised questions about whether the Qatar aircraft and towing crew followed their instructions, the investigation will need to establish the sequence of clearances, communications and movements before responsibility can be determined.

Air traffic restrictions add to the concern

The near-collision occurred against a backdrop of operational difficulties at Sydney Airport.

Air traffic control was operating under restrictions between 6am and 8am on Sunday, reducing the number of aircraft that could move through the airport. The restrictions followed a period of disruption linked to air traffic-control staffing and rostering problems.

More than 150 flights were affected by disruptions in the preceding days, adding pressure to an airport where multiple runways, taxiways and aircraft movements must be carefully coordinated. Airservices Australia has acknowledged the operational challenges and is assisting investigators.

Former Jetstar pilot David Oliver described the latest incident as unusual, noting that aircraft movements at Sydney are normally managed through highly coordinated procedures.

The circumstances will now be examined by investigators, who are expected to review recorded communications, aircraft and ground-movement data and interview the personnel involved.

A second serious Sydney runway incident in weeks

The Jetstar-Qatar near-miss is particularly significant because it comes only weeks after another serious runway conflict involving two Qantas aircraft.

On July 27, a Qantas 737 was cleared to cross runway 34L at Sydney Airport while a QantasLink Q400 was conducting its landing roll on the same runway.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) described the event as a “breakdown of co-ordination.” Air traffic control detected the conflict and warned both crews, with the 737 stopping after the holding point before the two aircraft came into contact.

Both Qantas aircraft were acting on ATC instructions, according to the airline, which said it would support the ATSB investigation.

The investigation is examining the actions of the controllers and pilots, as well as the recorded operational data surrounding the incident. It is expected to be completed later this year.

The proximity of the two events has intensified attention on Sydney's air traffic-control system, particularly staffing, training and workload.

An ATSB safety report published in July also recorded concerns about training and the transition to new Sydney airspace arrangements. CASA said it expected Airservices Australia to identify and manage safety risks associated with the transition, while the ATSB noted that previous safety reports had raised concerns involving staffing, supervision, training and change management within Sydney Terminal Control Unit.

Sydney has a longer history of runway conflicts

The latest incidents are not without precedent.

In 2019, the ATSB investigated a close-proximity occurrence at Sydney involving a Qantas Boeing 737, a Qantas Airbus A330 and a QantasLink Dash 8. The aircraft were operating in the complex environment created by Sydney's parallel runway operations.

An even more serious runway-incursion case occurred in August 2003. A catering vehicle accidentally entered runway 34L while an Airbus A330 was taking off. The aircraft passed directly over the vehicle after becoming airborne.

The ATSB found that the vehicle driver had become disorientated and entered the runway without clearance. The investigation identified the occurrence as a significant safety risk and examined the responsibilities of controllers, pilots and ground personnel in preventing runway incursions.

These earlier cases demonstrate why runway and taxiway coordination is so critical. A modern airport is a tightly choreographed environment in which aircraft, towing vehicles, ground crews and controllers must follow precise instructions. A breakdown at any point can rapidly create a collision risk.

Other recent Sydney safety investigations

Sydney has also featured in several recent ATSB investigations that, while not directly comparable to the Jetstar-Qatar incident, illustrate the range of operational risks faced by aircraft using the airport.

In July 2026, the ATSB released its final report into a September 2025 incident involving a Boeing 767 approaching Sydney. The aircraft descended well below the expected glideslope after its autopilot was affected when two Airbus A380s entered an area where they interfered with the instrument landing system signal. The aircraft eventually levelled off and conducted a missed approach.

The ATSB has also investigated a Qantas Boeing 737 engine failure during take-off from Sydney in November 2024. The aircraft suffered an engine failure after reaching take-off decision speed, continued the take-off and subsequently returned safely for a single-engine landing. The ATSB found that effective training and procedures contributed to the safe outcome.

These cases are fundamentally different from a runway or taxiway conflict, but they underline the importance of multiple layers of protection — pilot training, ATC procedures, airport systems and effective communication — when something goes wrong.

The question now is what happened between the instructions and the aircraft

The most important issue in the Jetstar-Qatar incident will be establishing the exact timeline.

Investigators will need to determine:

What instructions were issued to the Jetstar aircraft?

What instructions were given to the Qatar aircraft and its towing crew?

Were those instructions correctly understood and acknowledged?

Did either aircraft or the towing team deviate from its clearance?

What did the air traffic controller know about the positions of both aircraft?

How much warning did the Jetstar crew have before applying the brakes?

Were staffing or operational restrictions a contributing factor?

At this stage, it would be premature to conclude that either the pilots, ground crew or air traffic controllers were solely responsible.

What is clear is that the Jetstar pilots detected the developing conflict and stopped the aircraft before a collision occurred. That response prevented what could have been a much more serious accident.

A warning for one of Australia's busiest airports

The latest near-miss comes at a sensitive time for Sydney aviation.

With Western Sydney International Airport preparing for passenger operations later this year, Sydney's aviation network is undergoing a major transformation. Jetstar is scheduled to become the first airline to launch passenger services from the new airport in October, while Qantas will follow with passenger operations in 2027.

At the same time, Sydney Airport remains one of Australia's most intensively used aviation facilities.

The Jetstar-Qatar incident therefore raises questions that extend beyond the two aircraft involved. If investigators find that communication, staffing, training or procedural weaknesses contributed to the near-collision, those issues will need to be addressed before another close call becomes an accident.

For now, the investigation will determine whether Sunday's event was an isolated breakdown or part of a wider operational problem.

Two aircraft came dangerously close on the ground. A Jetstar crew member was injured. And, once again, an airport designed around precision coordination is being asked to explain how that coordination broke down.

text:
eSAF Blended With Conventional Jet Fuel To Meet Specifications

American Airlines and Infinium announced the first use of electro sustainable aviation fuel (eSAF) on an American flight that departed Corpus Christi International Airport (CRP) and landed at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW), demonstrating the real-world deployment of next-generation, drop-in sustainable aviation fuel.

The airline said the flight marks a transition from innovation to implementation, signaling a new phase in scaling viable, low-carbon alternatives to conventional jet fuel and advancing the future of sustainable flight.

The eSAF used for the flight was part of a batch produced and blended at Infinium’s Pathfinder facility in Corpus Christi, Texas — the world’s first commercial-scale power-to-liquids eFuels production site, which has been operating since 2023. The eSAF batch was blended with conventional jet fuel and tested to meet the ASTM International specification for JetA, certifying its use in today’s aircraft engines and fueling infrastructure without further modification. It was then delivered to the common jet fuel tanks at CRP before being allocated to American’s flight to DFW — the first delivery of SAF made without biobased feedstocks to a commercial airport in the U.S. The flight demonstrates the compatibility of eSAF with existing aviation jet fuel supply chains.

Infinium’s eSAF is made using waste CO? and renewable electricity, delivering a meaningful reduction in lifecycle greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions compared to conventional jet fuel. Infinium’s eSAF can reduce lifecycle GHG emissions by over 90% compared to conventional petroleum-based jet fuel.

"This flight represents a significant moment for aviation,"said American’s CEO Robert Isom. "Through our partnership with Infinium, we're demonstrating how next -generation technologies like eSAF can move from early investment to real-world application. Scaling SAF production at lower prices is essential to reducing emissions, strengthening our long-term competitiveness, and continuing to deliver the connectivity and economic benefits that our customers rely on."

Según relató, la primera experiencia fue en 2024 y, desde entonces, el cultivo fue ocupando un lugar cada vez más importante dentro del esquema agrícola.
Otra de las experiencias compartidas correspondió al sudeste bonaerense, donde el agrónomo Pablo Calviño expuso los resultados obtenidos con camelina y colza.
text:
ROSARIO.- Lo que hace apenas unos años aparecía como una alternativa incipiente para diversificar las rotaciones hoy comienza a consolidarse como una nueva herramienta productiva para el agro argentino. La incorporación de colza, cártamo y camelina gana terreno campaña tras campaña y ya permitió alcanzar en 2026 unas 160.000 hectáreas certificadas dentro del programa que impulsa Bunge, una estrategia que busca intensificar el uso del suelo, generar nuevos ingresos para los productores y responder a la creciente demanda internacional de materias primas con menor huella de carbono.

El avance de estos cultivos de invierno fue uno de los ejes de una charla técnica organizada por la compañía durante el Congreso de Aapresid, donde productores, asesores y especialistas compartieron experiencias sobre el manejo agronómico de estas oleaginosas y analizaron las oportunidades comerciales que comienzan a abrirse para el sector.

Campaña 2026/27: con mejores precios, un año Niño y más tecnología, el productor vuelve a apostar fuerte por el maíz

Según explicaron, el crecimiento registrado en los últimos años responde a una combinación de factores: la necesidad de aprovechar períodos tradicionalmente destinados al barbecho, mejorar la salud del suelo, diversificar los sistemas productivos y abastecer mercados que exigen materias primas cada vez más sustentables.

Al abrir la jornada, Jorge Bassi, director de Marketing y Nuevos Negocios de Bunge Argentina, destacó que cualquier transformación productiva solo puede construirse junto a quienes producen.

“Es la oportunidad” o “paso a paso”: diputados del PRO y LLA dejaron expuesta una diferencia sobre los tiempos para terminar con las retenciones

“Lanzamos planes y programas, pero quien está en el campo y arriesga el capital es el productor. Por eso, todo lo que hacemos parte de trabajar junto a ellos y generar herramientas que permitan producir más y, al mismo tiempo, hacerlo de una manera cada vez más sustentable”, afirmó.

Según explicó, la empresa comenzó hace cuatro años a desarrollar un programa basado en la incorporación de oleaginosas de invierno con un doble objetivo: incrementar la productividad y mejorar los indicadores ambientales de los sistemas agrícolas.

“Intensificar la agricultura nos permite generar un doble impacto: reemplazar un período de barbecho por un cultivo que genera renta y, al mismo tiempo, dejar más carbono en el suelo, cuidando su estructura”, sostuvo.

Bassi señaló que esta estrategia forma parte de una agenda más amplia vinculada con la descarbonización de la producción agropecuaria y la transición energética, donde la agricultura tiene un papel cada vez más relevante como proveedora de materias primas para los biocombustibles. “La agricultura también es parte de la transición del transporte, porque puede ser una fuente de materias primas para los biocombustibles y ayudar al transporte a reducir sus emisiones”, indicó.

En ese contexto, destacó el crecimiento que viene mostrando el mercado del Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), el combustible sostenible para aviación, cuya expansión demandará aceites con una huella de carbono cada vez menor.

“La demanda de aceites para la industria de SAF está creciendo y, para estas empresas, la certificación es fundamental, ya que el principal factor es la huella de carbono de la materia prima y cómo fue producida”, explicó.

Para el directivo, ese escenario obliga a pensar la producción desde una lógica diferente. Ya no alcanza con producir más, sino que también será necesario demostrar cómo fue producido cada cultivo y bajo qué estándares ambientales.

En ese sentido destacó que la estrategia impulsada por la compañía ya alcanzó durante 2026 unas 160.000 hectáreas certificadas entre colza, cártamo y camelina, una superficie que refleja el crecimiento que tuvieron estas alternativas dentro de los planteos agrícolas: “Es una manera de producir más, pero también de responder a una demanda que cada vez va a exigir materias primas con una menor huella de carbono”.

Para Bassi, la Argentina cuenta además con una ventaja diferencial respecto de otros países productores: la posibilidad de aprovechar inviernos que permiten incorporar estos cultivos sin reemplazar necesariamente a los tradicionales, sino ocupando períodos del año que antes permanecían improductivos.

Uno de los casos expuestos fue el del cártamo, un cultivo que comenzó a ganar espacio luego de las sucesivas campañas afectadas por la sequía. Miguel Kolar, asesor técnico de Agro Cotton Grupo Linke, contó que la decisión de incorporarlo surgió a partir de la necesidad de replantear el sistema productivo: “Tuvimos que replantearnos nuestro modelo productivo y buscar alternativas que nos permitieran hacer una agricultura más resiliente”.

Según relató, la primera experiencia fue en 2024 y, desde entonces, el cultivo fue ocupando un lugar cada vez más importante dentro del esquema agrícola. Hoy el grupo siembra unas 15.000 hectáreas de cártamo sobre un total de 20.000 hectáreas, una superficie que refleja el crecimiento alcanzado: “Es una superficie muy significativa para nosotros y demuestra la importancia que fue adquiriendo este cultivo dentro de nuestro modelo productivo”. Kolar destacó además que el cártamo permitió mantener al maíz dentro de la rotación y realizar un uso más eficiente de los recursos al complementar ambos cultivos.

La experiencia con colza también mostró resultados alentadores. Matías Taravella, asesor técnico de Jakas SA, explicó que comenzaron a trabajar con este cultivo hace tres años en una región caracterizada por largos períodos de barbecho: “Hemos logrado lotes de hasta 30 quintales por hectárea con cosecha directa, lo que demuestra que es un cultivo que tiene un muy buen potencial productivo para nuestra región”.

Más allá de los rindes, destacó el impacto positivo sobre el suelo. Explicó que, luego de la cosecha, la colza deja una estructura más mullida que favorece la infiltración del agua y mejora las condiciones para los cultivos siguientes: “La incorporación de cultivos de invierno nos permite pensar en un sistema más intensivo, en el que podamos hacer más cultivos durante el año y aprovechar mejor los recursos que tenemos disponibles”.

Otra de las experiencias compartidas correspondió al sudeste bonaerense, donde el agrónomo Pablo Calviño expuso los resultados obtenidos con camelina y colza. Explicó que el principal aporte de estos cultivos consiste en ocupar un período del año que antes permanecía sin producción, sin desplazar necesariamente a los cultivos tradicionales.

Y destacó que la soja de segunda implantada sobre camelina logra rindes muy similares a los de una soja de primera y que el costo de implantar este cultivo resulta prácticamente equivalente al de mantener un barbecho, con la diferencia de que el lote genera producción, ingresos y mejora el funcionamiento del sistema agrícola: “Lo interesante de estos cultivos es que no necesariamente vienen a reemplazar a los cultivos tradicionales, sino a ocupar un período que antes estaba vacío. Eso nos permite intensificar la producción y aprovechar mucho mejor cada hectárea”.

Más allá de las diferencias entre regiones y planteos productivos, las experiencias coincidieron en una conclusión: la incorporación de colza, cártamo y camelina deja de ser una alternativa experimental para convertirse en una herramienta que permite aumentar la intensidad de uso del suelo, mejorar la sustentabilidad de los sistemas y abrir nuevas oportunidades comerciales.

​Bunge presentó en Aapresid los avances de su programa de intensificación de rotaciones; en colza, camelina y cártamo se destacó una certificación que cubre esa superficie y, entre otros usos, una oportunidad para el combustible sostenible para aviación

title: United Airlines Marks 100 Years of Global Connectivity
description:
What started as a postal lifeline for remote communities quickly became part of a broader experiment in scheduled commercial aviation across the United States.
Publicly available historical accounts show that this consolidation created a coast-to-coast network and set the foundation for what would officially be known as United Air Lines in the early 1930s.
Through the mid-20th century, United expanded alongside the regulated U.S. airline industry, adding more routes, cabin services and aircraft types while operating under government-set fares and tightly controlled competition.
In the decades that followed, United used new aircraft types to build up a global network spanning Europe, Asia-Pacific and Latin America.
Behind the scenes, United has also embraced data-driven operations and more fuel-efficient aircraft to manage costs and reduce environmental impact.
text:
United Airlines is marking its 100th anniversary this year, a milestone that traces a path from a single airmail route over the American West to one of the world’s largest global carriers linking more than 400 destinations across six continents.

From Airmail Lifeline to National Route Network

United’s story begins on April 6, 1926, when Varney Air Lines launched contract airmail service between Pasco, Washington, Boise, Idaho and Elko, Nevada using open-cockpit biplanes. What started as a postal lifeline for remote communities quickly became part of a broader experiment in scheduled commercial aviation across the United States.

By the late 1920s and early 1930s, Varney Air Lines was folded into a larger aviation holding company that brought together Boeing Air Transport, Pacific Air Transport and National Air Transport. Publicly available historical accounts show that this consolidation created a coast-to-coast network and set the foundation for what would officially be known as United Air Lines in the early 1930s.

Through the mid-20th century, United expanded alongside the regulated U.S. airline industry, adding more routes, cabin services and aircraft types while operating under government-set fares and tightly controlled competition. The carrier became a symbol of the so-called “mainline” era, when aviation marketing emphasized speed, modernity and dependable scheduled service for both business and leisure travelers.

After U.S. deregulation in 1978, United restructured its network around hubs such as Chicago O’Hare, Denver and San Francisco, a model that allowed it to consolidate traffic and offer more frequent connections. Industry analyses indicate that this hub-and-spoke architecture remains central to United’s business, supporting dense domestic coverage and feeding a growing portfolio of international flights.

Jet Age Firsts and Global Alliances

United was among the early adopters of jet aircraft, introducing the Boeing 720 and later expanding into larger widebody types that opened transcontinental and transoceanic routes. Aviation museum records highlight how the shift from propeller-driven aircraft to jets dramatically reduced travel times and reshaped expectations for long-distance journeys.

In the decades that followed, United used new aircraft types to build up a global network spanning Europe, Asia-Pacific and Latin America. Historical timetables and industry timelines show that the airline steadily added long-haul services from major U.S. hubs, linking business centers such as London, Tokyo and Frankfurt while also opening routes to tourism destinations across the Caribbean and beyond.

United’s international reach expanded further in 1997, when it became one of the founding members of Star Alliance, now one of the world’s largest airline groupings. Through that alliance, United customers gained access to coordinated schedules, loyalty benefits and through-ticketing on partner carriers, helping the airline offer one-stop connections to hundreds of additional cities that it does not serve with its own aircraft.

Today, commercially available fleet and schedule data indicate that United operates more than a thousand mainline and regional aircraft, with hubs in key U.S. and Pacific locations and an especially strong presence at Newark, San Francisco, Chicago, Houston and Washington Dulles. The network mirrors broader trends in global mobility, supporting both corporate travel and a rapidly growing segment of international leisure tourism.

Innovation in Passenger Experience and Operations

Across its first century, United has repeatedly used technology and new service concepts to differentiate its product and operations. Early innovations included the deployment of dedicated flight attendants in the United States, coordinated timetable planning and the adoption of advanced navigation and weather systems that improved reliability on long routes over mountainous and coastal terrain.

In the modern era, the airline has invested in premium long-haul cabins, branded lounge experiences and digital tools that allow travelers to manage bookings, tracking and rebooking directly from mobile devices. Publicly available information on recent fleet upgrades points to a focus on lie-flat business class seating on intercontinental flights, enhanced entertainment systems and in-flight connectivity aimed at both business and leisure passengers.

Behind the scenes, United has also embraced data-driven operations and more fuel-efficient aircraft to manage costs and reduce environmental impact. Industry research into airline networks notes that large carriers, including United, use complex scheduling systems and real-time analytics to minimize disruptions, optimize aircraft utilization and adapt capacity to seasonal demand spikes.

The airline’s centennial year has become a showcase for these passenger and operational upgrades, with special liveries, onboard amenity designs and branded merchandise highlighting milestones from its early airmail days through the jet age and into today’s connected, digital-first travel landscape.

Sustainability Commitments and Future-Focused Technology

United’s 100th anniversary is unfolding at a time of heightened scrutiny over aviation’s environmental impact, and the company has positioned itself as an early mover on several fronts. Published corporate materials and independent coverage note that United has invested in sustainable aviation fuel production, including commercial-scale deployments on selected routes, as well as equity stakes in emerging fuel and propulsion technologies.

The carrier has announced long-term goals to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, in part by supporting the development of sustainable aviation fuel, more efficient aircraft and potential future innovations such as hydrogen or electric-powered regional flight concepts. These commitments fit within a broader push by the airline industry to align with national and international climate objectives while continuing to accommodate growing demand for air travel.

United’s fleet strategy also reflects this balancing act. Orders for new-generation narrowbody and widebody aircraft are designed to replace older jets with models that burn less fuel per seat, potentially lowering both operating costs and emissions. Analysts of the U.S. air transportation network point out that such fleet renewals can deliver meaningful environmental gains when applied at scale across thousands of daily flights.

As United celebrates a century of operations, these sustainability measures are becoming central to its messaging about the future of travel. The airline’s centennial campaigns are expected to highlight both its historical role in connecting communities and its efforts to make those connections more environmentally responsible in the decades ahead.

A Century of Connections Shaping Travel Patterns

United’s growth from a western airmail route to a global network carrier has helped reshape how Americans and international travelers think about distance and time. By linking small and mid-sized communities to major hubs, the airline has played a part in making same-day business trips, spontaneous weekend breaks and complex multi-stop itineraries more accessible to a broad range of passengers.

Academic studies of air transportation networks describe how large carriers create dense clusters of connectivity around hub airports, enabling thousands of possible itineraries off a single bank of arrivals and departures. United’s role at major U.S. hubs contributes to this effect, turning cities like Chicago, Denver and Houston into gateways for domestic and international flows of people and commerce.

The centennial also underscores how closely airline fortunes are tied to wider economic and geopolitical trends. United’s history includes prolonged periods of growth alongside global tourism booms, but also downturns, restructurings and strategic pivots in response to recessions, fuel price shocks and public health crises. Each phase has left a mark on route maps, fleet composition and service offerings.

As it enters its second century, United is positioning its legacy as a competitive advantage, emphasizing both its status as one of the oldest continuously operating U.S. carriers and its ongoing investment in technologies aimed at making flying more efficient, connected and sustainable. For travelers, the anniversary is a reminder that every routine boarding call sits atop a century of experimentation, consolidation and innovation that continues to shape how the world moves.

text:
Energi Hijau dari Pesisir: Kelapa sebagai Bahan Bakar Masa Depan dan Penakluk Stratosfer

Dalam ekosistem Industri Terpadu 5F, sebuah pabrik raksasa yang memproses pangan, pakan, serat, dan pupuk tentu membutuhkan pasokan listrik dan energi panas yang sangat masif. Apakah kita masih harus bergantung pada minyak bumi atau batu bara fosil yang mengotori udara? Jawabannya ada pada huruf "F" yang kelima, yakni Fuel (Bahan Bakar).

Dalam konsep industri 5F yang presisi, produk-produk turunan biomassa padat seperti briket, biopellet, dan biocoal (biobatu bara) secara ketat diklasifikasikan sebagai pilar bahan bakar (Fuel). Kelapa sejatinya adalah "baterai alam" penyimpan energi matahari yang mampu disulap menjadi bahan bakar roket industri hingga tiket bebas emisi penerbangan global.

Menyalakan Jantung Pabrik: Biodiesel CNO dan Gasifikasi Syngas

Untuk memutar turbin generator listriknya, pabrik 5F mengandalkan dua senjata energi yang diproduksi dari limbahnya sendiri:

Biodiesel CNO: Minyak kelapa mentah (Coconut Natural Oil) dieksploitasi melalui proses transesterifikasi basa yang memecah trigliserida dengan efisiensi konversi mencapai 98%. Hasilnya adalah biodiesel murni dengan angka setana di atas 65, tetap cair pada suhu -5 C, dan mampu memangkas emisi gas rumah kaca 60-70% lebih rendah dibandingkan diesel biasa.

Gasifikasi Syngas: Serpihan batok kelapa bahkan hanya sabut kelapa diproses dalam fluidized bed gasifier bersuhu 800 C melalui injeksi udara dan uap yang presisi. Pemecahan ikatan karbon ini menghasilkan Gas Sintetis (Syngas) yang kaya Hidrogen, Karbon Monoksida, dan Metana. Dengan efisiensi termal 75%, gas ini memutar generator pabrik dan menghasilkan 850-950 kWh listrik per ton biomassa.

Revolusi Bahan Bakar Padat: Briket Premium dan Biocoal

Sisa-sisa biomassa padat dari pengolahan kelapa diproses secara khusus untuk menggantikan dominasi energi kotor. Dalam pilar Fuel ini, produk-produk tersebut sangat krusial bagi industri berat:

Briket Arang Premium: Arang tempurung kelapa dipadatkan menjadi briket premium yang menyala dengan kepadatan kalori di atas 7.000~kcal/kg. Briket tanpa asap dan abu ini merajai pasar ekspor global untuk pemanas ruangan, BBQ di Eropa, hingga kebutuhan Shisha di Timur Tengah. Sebagian arang ini juga diaktivasi uap menjadi Activated Carbon dengan luas permukaan pori melebihi 1.000 meter persegi per gram, yang sangat vital untuk filter penjernih air industri.

Inovasi Biocoal (Biobatu Bara): Serpihan sabut pendek dan pelepah dipanggang tanpa oksigen pada suhu 200-300 C (torefaksi). Hasilnya adalah bongkahan pelet hitam (Black Pellet) yang keras, tahan air, dan mudah terbakar seperti batu bara fosil kualitas tinggi. Biocoal ini menjadi solusi elegan (co-firing) untuk mematikan ketergantungan PLTU dan industri semen pada batu bara perusak bumi.

Bioavtur Stratosfer: Menyelamatkan Kelapa Reject

Dunia penerbangan komersial saat ini didesak untuk menggunakan Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) guna menghindari denda emisi karbon yang berat. Kelapa hadir sebagai penyelamat melalui inovasi yang sangat membanggakan:

Kelapa yang bentuknya kerdil, rusak (reject), berjamur, atau tidak lolos seleksi makanan dimanfaatkan minyaknya.

Molekul asam lemak kelapa (rantai C11-C12) yang identik dengan bahan bakar jet pesawat diretas melalui reaktor tekanan ekstrem (hidrodeoksigenasi/HDO) dengan suntikan gas hidrogen dan katalis Nikel-Molibdenum.

Bioavtur sintetis ini memiliki titik beku hingga minus 59,41 C, menjadikannya bahan bakar yang sangat andal untuk pesawat komersial yang melintasi dinginnya stratosfer.

Pack Carburizing: Memperkuat Baja dari Arang Batok

Pilar bahan bakar dari kelapa bahkan mampu menembus industri peleburan logam. Baja karbon rendah (seperti ST37) yang murah namun lunak bisa diperkuat menggunakan sisa pembakaran batok kelapa:

Melalui metode Pack Carburizing, baja lunak dikurung bersama serbuk arang tempurung kelapa dan dipanaskan hingga 900 C.

Atom karbon dari arang menyusup dan mengunci pori-pori permukaan baja.

Setelah didinginkan secara mendadak (quenching), kekerasan baja melonjak drastis hingga 54,21 HRC, menjadikannya baja super yang siap digunakan untuk girboks maupun alat berat pertanian.

Saatnya The Tree of Life Mengubah Wajah Bioekonomi Indonesia

Perjalanan membedah anatomi The Tree of Life telah membawa kita pada satu kesadaran baru: dari jejak peradaban kuno di Candi Borobudur hingga teknologi biorefinery masa depan, kelapa selalu menjadi anugerah terbesar bagi Nusantara. Selama bertahun-tahun, kita tertidur dan membiarkan harta karun ini diekspor bulat-bulat sebagai bahan mentah, sementara nilai tambahnya dikeruk oleh bangsa lain.

Kini, saatnya kita terbangun. Implementasi Industri Terpadu dengan urutan ekosistem yang presisi Food, Feed, Fiber, Fertilizer, dan Fuel adalah sebuah game changer. Model ekonomi sirkular paripurna ini memastikan tidak ada satu gram pun bagian pohon yang terbuang menjadi sampah (Zero Waste). Kita hadir dengan The Ultimate Trilemma Solver, mematahkan mitos bahwa kita harus memilih antara mengisi perut manusia, memberi makan ternak, atau menyalakan mesin pabrik. Semuanya bisa terpenuhi secara harmonis.

Lebih dari sekadar mengejar profitabilitas, ekosistem 5F adalah wujud nyata pencapaian Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) dunia dan pemenuhan standar tata kelola ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance). Dengan menyerap jutaan ton emisi karbon, memberdayakan koperasi petani lokal, dan menghasilkan energi bersih, kita sedang membangun benteng kedaulatan bangsa.

Cetak biru teknologi hijau ini sejatinya adalah pondasi untuk sebuah pergerakan yang jauh lebih masif. Kerangka circular economy yang tangguh ini tidak hanya berhenti pada kelapa, melainkan menjadi prototipe yang siap direplikasi untuk komoditas strategis lainnya mulai dari Sagu 5F, Sawit 5F, hingga Padi 5F. Inilah cetak biru mutlak untuk memerangi climate change sekaligus mewujudkan swasembada pangan, pakan, papan, pupuk, dan energi secara holistik di tanah air.

text:
PT Pertamina (Persero) menerapkan strategi pertumbuhan ganda atau Dual Growth Strategy untuk menjaga ketahanan energi nasional sekaligus mendukung transisi energi berkelanjutan, sebagaimana dilansir dari Detik Finance.

Langkah strategis tersebut berfokus pada dua pilar utama, yakni memaksimalkan bisnis inti migas (Maximizing Legacy Business) dan membangun bisnis rendah karbon (Building Low Carbon Business).

Presiden RI Prabowo Subianto menegaskan bahwa kemandirian sektor energi menjadi kunci utama bagi keberlangsungan serta kedaulatan bangsa Indonesia di tengah ketidakpastian global.

"Negara yang sebesar kita kalau masih mau merdeka, kalau masih mau survive bertahan hidup, mau tidak mau kita harus mandiri dan energi adalah salah satu bidang yang sangat menentukan," ujar Prabowo.

Menanggapi arahan tersebut, manajemen BUMN energi ini mengoptimalkan seluruh aset produksi hulu guna memastikan ketersediaan pasokan dalam negeri.

"Menjawab kebutuhan dan tantangan dimaksud, Pertamina menjalankan Dual Growth Strategy yang berfokus pada dua pilar utama, yakni Maximizing Legacy Business dan Building Low Carbon Business," kata Wakil Direktur Utama Pertamina, Oki Muraza.

Guna memperkuat lini hulu migas, perusahaan menggenjot operasional aset domestik demi mempertahankan tingkat produksi minyak dan gas bumi.

"Setiap peningkatan produksi dari lapangan migas merupakan kontribusi nyata Pertamina dalam memperkuat ketahanan energi nasional. Melalui pengelolaan aset yang semakin andal, efisien, dan berkelanjutan, Pertamina terus mendukung pencapaian target produksi migas nasional," ucap Oki.

Hingga akhir semester I 2026, PT Pertamina Hulu Energi (PHE) mencatatkan produksi migas sebesar 935 ribu barel setara minyak per hari (MBOEPD). Capaian ini terdiri atas produksi minyak 459 ribu barel per hari (MBOPD) dan gas 2.756 juta kaki kubik per hari (MMSCFD).

Peningkatan kinerjanya ditopang penuntasan pengeboran 278 sumur eksploitasi, 601 kegiatan workover, serta 13.870 well service selama Januari hingga Juni 2026. Eksplorasi PHE juga menghasilkan penemuan sumber daya kontingen 2C sebesar 108 MMBOE dan cadangan terbukti P1 sebesar 24,9 MMBOE.

Di sektor pengolahan, efisiensi dan kapasitas kilang ditingkatkan melalui proyek perluasan seperti Refinery Development Master Plan (RDMP) Balikpapan.

"Selain memastikan kehandalan kilang, Pertamina juga melakukan peningkatan kompleksitas kilang. Salah satunya melalui proyek Refinery Development Master Plan (RDMP) Balikpapan. Proyek yang akan meningkatkan kualitas produk yang dihasilkan menjadi setara euro 5," kata Oki.

Enam kilang Pertamina yang beroperasi saat ini memiliki kapasitas olah minyak mentah hingga 1,1 juta barel per hari untuk menghasilkan BBM, LPG, Avtur, dan Petrokimia.

Pada pilar bisnis rendah karbon, perusahaan mengakselerasi pengembangan produk nabati, seperti penerapan mandatori B50 sejak awal Juli serta pengembangan biofuel.

"Pertamina berkomitmen mendukung program pemerintah dalam hal pengoptimalan sumber daya alam nabati untuk mendukung ketahanan energi. Sejak awal Juli, Pemerintah menetapkan B50 mandatori. Dan Pertamina menjadi salah satu bagian penting dalam menjalankan kebijakan pemerintah tersebut.

Inovasi bahan bakar ramah lingkungan juga diwujudkan melalui peluncuran Pertamina Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) berbasis minyak goreng bekas yang memangkas emisi karbon hingga 84 persen.

"Teknologi SAF ini sepenuhnya dikembangkan oleh insinyur dalam negeri, membuktikan kapasitas Indonesia sebagai regional champion energi hijau," kata Oki.

Pengembangan bisnis rendah karbon tersebut turut mencakup dekarbonisasi, teknologi CCUS/CCS, ekspansi panas bumi, hingga jaringan gas rumah tangga dan infrastruktur SPKLU.
