text:
A new deep-water renewable energy project came online Thursday as China activated its inaugural tension-leg floating wind farm.

Operated by the China National Offshore Oil Corp (CNOOC), the 16-megawatt Haiyou Anlan platform currently feeds clean electricity straight into the Lufeng oilfield grid. The installation holds the global record for the largest TLP wind site by capacity while sitting at a greater depth and distance from the coast than similar projects.

Located within the Pearl River Mouth Basin, the platform is anchored 85 miles offshore and 124 miles southeast of Shenzhen in Guangdong province. The waters at the site reach 136 metres deep. Rising as high as a 110-storey skyscraper, the structure includes a robust turbine built to endure Level 17 typhoons throughout its estimated 25 years of service.

Output from the site should hit roughly 54mn kilowatt-hours of power each year. This generation capacity will cut annual fuel oil use by 15,000 cubic metres and drop carbon dioxide emissions by 35,000 tonnes.

Tackling complex offshore engineering

Rather than using standard foundations fixed directly to the ocean floor, tension-leg designs rely on floating hulls tethered to the seabed by vertical cables. This setup restricts swaying caused by rough currents. Although these systems provide better stability and use less steel per megawatt than semi-submersible units, their construction requires exacting precision.

The Haiyou Anlan weighs 7,800 tonnes and its blades sweep a space roughly the size of seven football pitches. CNOOC engineers relied on custom high-strength moorings and 3D marine condition simulators to ensure millimetre-accurate underwater assembly.

Shifting focus to eastern power demands

Xiamen University energy economics director Lin Boqiang told the Global Times that this development indicates where the offshore wind sector is heading. Pushing past shallow coastal zones lets energy firms capture the heavier and more reliable wind speeds found far out at sea.

Building these facilities remains expensive despite local progress in manufacturing large turbines. Yet Lin pointed out the strategic need to boost green energy production in eastern China. The nation currently sees its highest industrial and residential power demand along the east coast, while its main solar and wind assets sit in remote western areas. Establishing deep-water farms allows developers to route clean energy directly to these coastal populations, cutting down reliance on long-distance transmission lines crossing the country.

Beijing is concurrently expanding its wider renewable fuel industry. On Wednesday, the National Energy Administration reported that domestic annual green fuel capacity reached 8mn tonnes of oil equivalent by the close of 2025. This figure covers sustainable aviation fuel alongside green ammonia and green methanol.

title: Middle East Travel and Tourism Faces 2026 Shock but WTTC Forecasts a Powerful Decade ...
description:
WTTC expects the Middle East to be the only global region where travel and tourism GDP declines during 2026.
WTTC Predicts the World’s Fastest Tourism Growth Through 2036 WTTC’s most consequential finding lies beyond the immediate downturn.
It forecasts that the Middle East will become the fastest-growing travel and tourism region globally between 2026 and 2036.
The Oman NCSI tourism portal and its official 2026 tourism statistical bulletin provide the principal national evidence.
The World Travel & Tourism Council predicts a drop in GDP mainly because of fighting, limited air travel and less movement of people.
text:
The travel and tourism economy in the Middle East is facing a challenge. New research from the World Travel & Tourism Council predicts a decline in the region in 2026 because of conflicts, limited air space and problems with moving people. This comes after an increase in 2025. However the same report says the Middle East will grow faster than any part of the world in the next ten years. This difference is important for airlines, hotels, people who invest money places that want to attract visitors and the people who travel. Government information from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Oman and Qatar shows that building structures meeting customer needs and plans to expand different areas are still going on. These efforts are creating a base, for recovery when things get better.

Middle East Travel and Tourism Enters a Critical Turning Point

The latest outlook from the World Travel & Tourism Council, published on 6 August 2026, presents one of the sharpest regional reversals in its current global forecast. It predicts that the economic contribution of Middle Eastern travel and tourism will fall from approximately US$386 billion in 2025 to US$330 billion in 2026.

That would represent a contraction of 14.5 per cent. WTTC expects the Middle East to be the only global region where travel and tourism GDP declines during 2026. The estimate reflects exceptional operating conditions rather than a normal cooling of consumer demand.

Conflict, airspace restrictions, flight disruption and changes in international passenger flows have affected a region that functions as a bridge between Asia, Europe and Africa. WTTC calculates that Middle Eastern aviation hubs handle about 14 per cent of international passengers worldwide, equivalent to roughly one in every seven international travellers.

This exposure amplifies the economic effect of aviation disruption. A traveller who changes an itinerary may remove spending from an airline, airport, hotel, restaurant, attraction and ground-transport provider during the same journey. A connecting passenger may also form part of several businesses revenue chains even without leaving an airport.

The downturn therefore reaches beyond traditional holiday travel. It affects corporate trips, conventions, international events, stopovers, airport retail, cargo-linked business journeys and investments tied to projected visitor volumes.

However, the 2026 contraction remains a forecast, not a completed annual result. Its eventual scale will depend on travel conditions, airline capacity, airspace availability, traveller confidence and the speed at which disrupted routes can be restored. WTTC’s official Middle East outlook should consequently be read as a scenario based on the information available when its research was prepared.

The 2026 Forecast Follows Strong Regional Growth in 2025

The severity of the predicted fall becomes clearer when set against the previous year. WTTC’s April 2026 Economic Impact Research estimated that Middle East travel and tourism grew by 5.3 per cent in 2025, exceeding estimated global sector growth of 4.1 per cent.

The sector generated approximately US$385.8 billion in regional GDP and supported around 7.1 million jobs in 2025. International visitor expenditure reportedly grew by 5.2 per cent, while business travel spending increased by approximately 23 per cent.

These figures describe a region that entered 2026 with substantial economic momentum. They also show why the expected contraction should not be interpreted as evidence that long-term tourism strategies had already failed.

Much of the 2025 expansion came from increased air connectivity, hospitality development, destination marketing, major events and government programmes designed to broaden economies beyond hydrocarbons. Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Oman and Qatar contributed strongly to this expansion, although their tourism systems differ considerably.

Saudi Arabia is building a large domestic and international tourism economy across multiple destinations. The UAE has mature aviation, hotel, retail and events ecosystems. Qatar is using sport, business events and stopover travel to extend the value of its infrastructure. Oman is taking a more measured approach centred on nature, heritage, hospitality and regional connectivity.

The 2025 results provide an essential baseline. Without that context, the 2026 forecast could appear to describe structural decline. Instead, official evidence indicates that a fast-expanding sector has encountered a major external disruption. WTTC’s 2025 regional assessment confirms the strength of the preceding year.

Airspace Disruption Is the Central Transmission Channel

The Middle East aviation network is integral to regional tourism. Large hubs connect long-haul traffic between continents, while growing regional airlines distribute passengers to secondary destinations. Airspace restrictions therefore have consequences far beyond the borders immediately affected.

The International Civil Aviation Organization reported significant regional airspace disruption in 2026. ICAO material presented at its Middle East planning and safety meetings recorded closures, restrictions and operational uncertainty across several flight information regions.

A subsequent ICAO regional report showed that daily traffic fell from approximately 5,100 flights to 1,677 flights at the onset of the disruption between late February and the end of May. This represented a reduction approaching 67 per cent before traffic began recovering.

Airlines operating through available corridors faced longer routes, additional coordination requirements and tactical air-traffic-management pressure. Oman’s Muscat Flight Information Region remained available for civil operations, but rerouted traffic affected its airspace and operating environment.

These conditions can increase flight times and fuel consumption. They can also reduce the number of rotations an aircraft can complete, complicate crew scheduling and weaken the reliability of onward connections.

For travellers, the practical consequences include revised departure times, longer journeys, missed connections, reduced frequency and higher uncertainty. For destinations, the effects may include fewer short-stay visitors, weaker last-minute bookings and lower demand from markets that depend on one-stop connections.

ICAO’s work on a harmonised regional contingency framework is therefore directly relevant to tourism recovery. The framework is designed to preserve safe and orderly traffic flows when normal air-navigation services are disrupted. It cannot remove geopolitical risk, but it can improve coordination and operational continuity. ICAO’s Middle East regional aviation documentation records the scale of the disruption.

Airlines Face Higher Costs Even Where Demand Remains

The International Air Transport Association’s June 2026 outlook reinforces the connection between airspace disruption and tourism performance. IATA forecast that global airline passenger demand would still grow during 2026, but at a slower pace than previously expected.

It projected a particularly deep Middle Eastern contraction. Regional passenger traffic, measured in revenue passenger kilometres, was forecast to fall by 11.4 per cent in 2026 as airspace restrictions and lost transfer traffic affected Middle Eastern carriers.

IATA reported that traffic carried by airlines registered in the Middle East fell 58.6 per cent year on year in March 2026. The decline moderated to 46.6 per cent in April, but the figures demonstrated how quickly airspace closures could interrupt established passenger flows.

The financial pressure extends beyond lost bookings. Longer routing raise fuel use. Restricted corridors reduce network efficiency. Flight cancellations create re accommodation and customer-service costs. Aircraft may also spend more time completing individual services, reducing productive utilisation.

IATA’s revised global forecast put airline profits at US$23 billion in 2026, down from US$45 billion in 2025. It attributed the deterioration partly to Middle East disruption and higher fuel costs. Global airline fuel expenditure was forecast to rise from US$252 billion to US$350 billion.

The impact is not confined to Middle Eastern companies. Airlines from Asia, Europe, Africa and the Americas use the region’s airports, airspace and connecting networks. Higher costs can influence fares, schedules and capacity decisions across international markets.

IATA nevertheless emphasises that the underlying willingness to travel had moderated rather than disappeared. That distinction supports the possibility of a strong recovery once routes become safer and more predictable. IATA’s official June 2026 air-transport outlook provides the wider operating context.

WTTC Predicts the World’s Fastest Tourism Growth Through 2036

WTTC’s most consequential finding lies beyond the immediate downturn. It forecasts that the Middle East will become the fastest-growing travel and tourism region globally between 2026 and 2036.

Regional travel and tourism GDP is projected to expand at an average annual rate of 6.3 per cent, reaching approximately US$605 billion by 2036. This would place growth well above the expected pace of the wider global economy.

Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Oman and Qatar form the centre of that long-range projection. WTTC estimated that these four markets generated a combined US$272 billion in travel and tourism GDP in 2025. Their combined contribution is forecast to reach US$435 billion by 2036.

A decade-long forecast should not be treated as a guaranteed result. Growth depends on security, investment discipline, demand, environmental constraints, labour supply, regulatory quality and the commercial performance of individual projects.

Nevertheless, the forecast is supported by assets that already exist. The region has major international hubs, modern airports, expanding airlines, substantial hotel inventories, large domestic markets, internationally recognised attractions and governments willing to invest in destination development.

WTTC estimated that Saudi Arabia generated US$178 billion in travel and tourism GDP during 2025, representing approximately 46 per cent of the Middle East total. Its sector reportedly grew 7.4 per cent, faster than both regional and global averages.

Travel and tourism accounted for an estimated 14.1 per cent of Saudi GDP under WTTC’s broad economic-impact methodology. That measure includes direct activity as well as supply-chain and induced effects, so it should not be confused with official measures of tourism’s direct contribution.

The UAE Retains a Mature and Highly Connected Visitor Economy

The United Arab Emirates tourism sector represents another major pillar of WTTC’s long-term forecast. WTTC estimated its travel and tourism economy at US$68.5 billion in 2025, supported by international visitor expenditure of approximately US$56.9 billion.

Its wider economic-impact assessment put travel and tourism at 11.9 per cent of UAE GDP and 13.6 per cent of employment. These figures reflect the sector’s reach through aviation, accommodation, retail, food services, entertainment and supporting supply chains.

Official UAE figures show that hotels welcomed more than 32 million guests during 2025, an increase of 5.1 per cent over 2024. Hotel-establishment revenue rose by 9.7 per cent to AED49.21 billion.

The rise in revenue exceeded guest growth, suggesting that value generation improved faster than headline volume. This matters because mature destinations increasingly need to raise visitor value, length of stay and spending rather than depend solely on ever-higher arrival totals.

Dubai recorded 19.59 million international overnight visitors in 2025, a five per cent annual increase and its third successive record year. It also retained a large and diversified accommodation market serving luxury, business, family, events and stopover segments.

The UAE’s exposure to aviation disruption is substantial because international connectivity is central to its economic model. Yet the same connectivity, global brand recognition and hotel capacity could support rapid recovery when operating conditions stabilise.

Its challenge is to preserve traveller trust during disruption. Accurate operational communication, flexible booking policies and coordination between airlines, airports, hotels and attractions can prevent a temporary interruption from becoming a longer reputational problem.

Oman’s Measured Growth Provides a Different Model

Oman occupies a smaller position in the regional tourism economy, but WTTC expects its contribution to rise from approximately US$7.9 billion to US$12 billion by 2036.

Its growth strategy differs from the region’s largest hub-led models. Oman’s tourism proposition relies heavily on landscapes, heritage, coastal experiences, nature, cultural assets and lower-density destination development.

Official statistics show steady expansion. Oman’s National Centre for Statistics and Information reported that three-to-five-star hotels received 2,376,955 guests in 2025, up 10.8 per cent from 2024.

Room nights climbed by 20.2 per cent to approximately 3.68 million. Revenue increased by 22.2 per cent to OMR297.3 million, while occupancy reached 56.7 per cent.

The faster increase in room nights than guests indicates longer or more intensive hotel use. Revenue growth also exceeded the rise in visitor numbers, which may indicate stronger room performance, additional spending or a changing accommodation mix.

Oman’s airspace acquired additional regional importance during the 2026 disruption. ICAO documentation noted that the Muscat Flight Information Region remained available for civil aviation, although altered traffic flows created additional routing and coordination demands.

This position offers opportunity and responsibility. Reliable air-navigation services can support regional continuity, but concentrated rerouting can place pressure on air-traffic systems and reduce operating efficiency.

Oman’s long-term success will depend on maintaining the qualities that distinguish it. Excessive or poorly located development could weaken the natural and cultural assets underlying demand. Growth therefore requires land-use planning, infrastructure, environmental management, community participation and consistent hospitality standards.

The Oman NCSI tourism portal and its official 2026 tourism statistical bulletin provide the principal national evidence.

Qatar Converts Major Events Into Repeatable Tourism Demand

Qatar welcomed 5.1 million international visitors in 2025, according to Qatar Tourism. This represented annual growth of 3.7 per cent and moved the country close to its stated target of attracting six million visitors annually by 2030.

Air arrivals accounted for 61 per cent of the total, land arrivals 32 per cent and sea arrivals seven per cent. The multi modal distribution gives Qatar more flexibility than a destination dependent entirely on aviation, although air access remains dominant.

The country sold more than 10.8 million room nights, an increase of 8.6 per cent. Average accommodation occupancy reached 71 per cent, while total accommodation revenue rose 12 per cent to QAR8.3 billion.

Qatar Tourism also reported more than one million international business visitors during 2025. Its events calendar included over 600 events, while tourism authorities activated more than 35 international partnerships and 95 marketing campaigns across 19 markets.

These figures show how Qatar is attempting to extend the legacy of major sporting infrastructure into a wider visitor economy. Business events, exhibitions, sport, culture, cruise calls and stopover products can generate demand across different seasons.

WTTC highlighted that international visitor spending represents 94.1 per cent of Qatar’s services exports. That concentration demonstrates tourism’s export importance, but it also exposes the economy to international mobility shocks.

The policy task is therefore twofold. Qatar must continue growing visitor demand while reducing its sensitivity to individual events or transport channels. A broader source-market mix, repeat visitation and integrated regional itineraries could support that objective.

Business Travel and MICE Remain Essential Growth Engines

Business travel was one of the Middle East’s strongest-performing tourism segments in 2025. WTTC estimated that regional business-travel spending increased by 23 per cent, while Saudi Arabia recorded growth exceeding 55 per cent.

This reflects an expanding calendar of investment conferences, exhibitions, corporate meetings, sporting events and government-led economic forums. New commercial activity attracts travellers who often spend more per day than leisure visitors and use airlines, premium hotels, restaurants and ground transport.

MICE demand also helps destinations manage seasonality. Conferences and exhibitions can be scheduled outside traditional holiday periods, supporting hotel occupancy and airline traffic during otherwise softer months.

The 2026 disruption exposes the segment’s sensitivity. organiser need predictable air access because delegates often travel for fixed dates and short stays. A disrupted connection can remove most of the value of a two-day conference trip.

Events may be postponed, shortened or moved when uncertainty affects speakers, exhibitors, insurance, freight or attendance. Even events that proceed can experience lower international participation.

Destinations can improve resilience by offering flexible contracting, hybrid participation, coordinated disruption policies and clear information about operational conditions. Regional collaboration can also help protect event calendars from avoidable clashes after postponed programmes are rescheduled.

Long term, the Middle East retains important MICE advantages: modern venues, strong aviation networks, substantial hotel capacity and government support. The central requirement is to ensure that event growth creates repeatable business relationships rather than temporary peaks in visitation.

Tourism Investment Must Be Judged by Returns, Not Announcements

WTTC reported 19.4 per cent growth in Saudi travel and tourism investment during 2025. Across the region, substantial capital continues to enter hotels, resorts, airports, attractions, entertainment venues and destination infrastructure.

This investment strengthens the long-range outlook, but a temporary decline in arrivals will test individual business plans. Projects based on uninterrupted high growth may face slower occupancy development, higher financing pressure or revised opening schedules.

The strongest projects will be those supported by realistic demand analysis, differentiated products, effective distribution and access to multiple visitor segments. Domestic tourism and regional travel can provide additional demand, but they should not be treated as automatic substitutes for long-haul international expenditure.

Investors will also need to distinguish between national growth and property-level performance. A destination can record rising arrivals while particular hotels or attractions struggle because supply expands faster than demand.

Revenue per available room, average length of stay, repeat visitation, visitor spending and operating margins are therefore more informative than arrival totals alone. Public authorities can support better decisions by publishing timely and granular statistics.

WTTC’s decade forecast creates a persuasive regional story, but it does not guarantee returns for every project. Commercial discipline remains essential, particularly when construction costs, fuel prices and financing conditions are volatile.

Employment Gains Could Be Tested by the Short-Term Contraction

Travel and tourism supported an estimated 7.1 million Middle Eastern jobs in 2025. These positions extend across accommodation, transport, food services, attractions, retail, events, technology and supply chains.

A 14.5 per cent contraction in sector GDP would not translate mechanically into an identical employment decline. Businesses may retain staff, reduce hours, postpone recruitment or absorb lower productivity while waiting for demand to recover.

However, small and medium-sized enterprises often have less financial capacity to manage prolonged disruption. Tour operators, independent restaurants, guides, event suppliers and transport businesses may experience pressure before larger companies.

Governments must therefore balance immediate resilience measures with long-term workforce development. Temporary support should be targeted and transparent, while training programmes should continue preparing residents for skilled tourism careers.

Saudi data demonstrate both opportunity and imbalance. Tourism employment exceeded one million in the third quarter of 2025, but Saudi nationals represented less than one-quarter of the measured workforce. Female workers represented a relatively small share in earlier 2025 data.

Increasing local and female participation can strengthen tourism’s social contribution. It can also build a larger domestic skills base capable of supporting expansion through 2036.

The quality of employment matters alongside quantity. Sustainable growth requires clear career pathways, fair conditions, recognised qualifications and productivity-enhancing technology. Without these foundations, rapid capacity expansion may produce labour shortages or inconsistent service.

Travellers Should Separate Regional Forecasts From Local Conditions

The Middle East is not a single operating environment. Conditions can differ significantly between countries, airports, routes and travel dates. A region-wide economic forecast should not be interpreted as a universal warning against travel.

Travellers should rely on current government advisories, airline notifications, airport information and official local guidance. They should verify routes shortly before departure because airspace restrictions can produce rapid schedule changes.

Passengers using connecting itineraries should allow additional time and avoid assuming that a previously reliable minimum connection will remain adequate. Keeping accommodation, transfers and onward tickets within flexible terms can reduce financial exposure.

Travel insurance should be examined carefully. Policies vary in their treatment of conflict, airspace closure, cancellation, missed connections and travel-advisory changes. Travellers should understand the exclusions before purchasing or changing an itinerary.

The 2026 disruption may also affect fares. Longer routing, reduced capacity and higher fuel costs can raise operating expenses even when flights continue. Conversely, particular destinations may offer promotional value if demand temporarily softens.

Clear distinctions matter. A cancelled route does not necessarily mean an airport is closed. A government advisory may apply to one area rather than an entire country. An economic forecast does not automatically describe the safety of an individual journey.

Responsible reporting should preserve these distinctions and avoid turning a complex regional disruption into an unsupported claim that every destination faces identical conditions.

Policy Coordination Will Determine the Speed of Recovery

WTTC argues that recovery will require cooperation between governments and the private sector. The official evidence supports this assessment because the disruption crosses national and commercial boundaries.

Civil aviation authorities must coordinate safe contingency routes. Airlines need timely operational information. Airports must manage changing passenger and aircraft flows. Tourism ministries must communicate accurately with source markets, while hotels and intermediaries need workable rebooking policies.

ICAO’s regional contingency framework provides a technical foundation for preserving aviation continuity. Its effectiveness depends on implementation, information sharing and coordination between states and air-navigation service providers.

Tourism authorities also need to avoid premature promotional claims. Confidence is strengthened by precise, verifiable information rather than assurances that ignore operational uncertainty.

Once conditions improve, restoring schedules will not be instantaneous. Airlines must reposition aircraft and crews, reopen sales, rebuild connecting banks and assess demand. Tour operators and event planners also need lead time.

Governments can accelerate recovery by simplifying temporary operational procedures, coordinating destination messaging and maintaining visa and border efficiency. However, safety must remain the central condition for capacity restoration.

The region’s previous investments create a strong base, but infrastructure cannot substitute for coordination. Airports, hotels and attractions generate value only when travellers can reach them reliably.

Economic Diversification Makes Tourism Too Important to Abandon

Tourism has become a central component of economic diversification across Gulf economies. The IMF has recognised that reforms have helped unlock growth in tourism, logistics, finance and renewable energy.

This strategy seeks to create private-sector jobs, attract foreign expenditure, stimulate investment and reduce dependence on hydrocarbon revenue. Tourism also supports aviation, construction, retail, culture, sport and entertainment.

The 2026 shock does not remove this logic. Instead, it demonstrates that diversification sectors carry their own risks. Tourism is exposed to conflict, health crises, climate conditions, consumer confidence and transport disruption.

Resilience therefore requires diversification within tourism itself. Countries need balanced source markets, domestic and international demand, leisure and business travel, different price segments and more than one transport gateway.

Fiscal discipline is equally important. Public investment should generate durable economic activity rather than depend indefinitely on subsidy. Private participation, transparent regulation and reliable data can improve allocation.

The long-term WTTC forecast suggests that tourism will remain a major growth sector. Yet the quality of expansion will matter as much as its scale. Projects that strengthen communities, protect assets and generate sustainable employment will carry greater long-term value than developments designed only to produce striking capacity figures.

Environmental and Social Pressures Will Grow With Recovery

A regional tourism economy approaching US$605 billion by 2036 would create substantial environmental and social demands. More flights, hotels, attractions and visitors would increase pressure on energy, water, land, waste systems and transport networks.

These constraints are especially important in arid destinations. Water-intensive landscaping, cooling requirements and large accommodation projects can raise resource use unless efficiency is embedded in design and operations.

Aviation growth also creates emissions challenges. Sustainable aviation fuel remains limited and expensive. IATA forecast that available SAF would equal only 0.8 per cent of global airline fuel consumption in 2026.

Destinations can reduce pressure through efficient buildings, public transport, renewable energy, water reuse, waste reduction and visitor management. Reliable measurement is essential because broad sustainability claims cannot replace documented performance.

Social considerations include access to tourism careers, community participation, cultural protection and the distribution of visitor spending. Rapid development can create impressive assets without producing equally broad local benefits.

Tourism strategies should therefore measure resident outcomes alongside arrivals and GDP. Employment quality, small-business participation, cultural preservation and infrastructure access are relevant indicators of success.

WTTC’s forecast offers a powerful economic opportunity. It also increases the urgency of managing growth before recovery accelerates.

What the WTTC Forecast Means for the Global Travel Industry

The Middle East’s position in intercontinental aviation means its 2026 contraction has global consequences. Airlines outside the region may gain traffic when passengers reroute, but longer journeys and constrained airspace can still raise system-wide costs.

European and Asian destinations may experience changes in connecting flows. African carriers and hubs may secure additional transfer demand. Tour operators may redesign itineraries, while corporate travel managers reconsider route resilience.

Hotels in unaffected destinations could gain diverted demand, but businesses tied to Middle Eastern outbound travellers may lose customers. The impact therefore varies across markets and cannot be summarized as a simple regional transfer of revenue.

For global tourism companies, the central lesson is that connectivity concentration creates efficiency during normal conditions but vulnerability during disruption. Network diversification, contingency planning and flexible inventory become strategic requirements.

For Middle Eastern destinations, the long-term opportunity remains considerable. The region combines capital, connectivity, growing attractions, expanding accommodation and policy commitment. Few regions possess all these elements simultaneously.

The immediate challenge is to preserve those advantages through a period of weaker activity. The decade ahead could validate WTTC’s forecast, but the pathway will depend on decisions made during the downturn.

Future Outlook for Middle East Travel and Tourism

Three indicators will reveal whether the projected recovery is taking hold.

The first is aviation restoration. Rising flight frequency, shorter routing and recovering transfer traffic would improve access and reduce costs.

The second is accommodation performance. Occupancy, room nights, revenue and length of stay will show whether visitor demand is returning across different destinations.

The third is investment delivery. Projects must open with sustainable financing, clear market positioning and sufficient demand rather than simply remain in announced pipelines.

National statistical agencies and tourism authorities should publish timely data so businesses can distinguish temporary volatility from structural change. Comparable regional measures would also improve decision-making.

WTTC’s forecast should be monitored rather than treated as a fixed destination. A 6.3 per cent average annual growth rate through 2036 is achievable only if operating stability returns and investment continues producing competitive experiences.

The Middle East tourism outlook is consequently neither a simple crisis story nor an uncomplicated boom narrative. It combines a severe near-term aviation shock with one of the strongest structural growth platforms in global tourism.

Conclusion

The Middle East travel and tourism industry is facing a disruption in 2026 but the proof does not say that its way of growing has failed. The World Travel & Tourism Council predicts a drop in GDP mainly because of fighting, limited air travel and less movement of people. Then the Middle East is expected to have the increase in tourism of any part of the world by 2036. Official numbers, from countries support the long-term picture: Saudi Arabia is building facilities the UAE still has a lot of visitors Oman is increasing its hotel services and Qatar is turning events into long stays. Recovery is not certain though. It will rely on air space, better information, good business practices, training workers and investing in places to visit.

[Source:- World Travel and Tourism Council]

title: Global SAF prices rise 10% as demand outpaces supply
description:
Global prices for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) increased by 10% in 2026 compared to the previous year.
According to BloombergNEF’s latest survey, the average SAF price reached $1,817/t, about five times higher than the price of conventional jet fuel.
Analysts say the increase was driven by higher conventional jet fuel prices following shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as stronger demand in markets with SAF blending mandates.
The UK and the European Union introduced a 2% SAF blending requirement in 2025, further supporting demand.
Global SAF production totaled 1.9 mln tons in 2025, covering only 0.6% of worldwide jet fuel demand.
text:
Global prices for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) increased by 10% in 2026 compared to the previous year. According to BloombergNEF’s latest survey, the average SAF price reached $1,817/t, about five times higher than the price of conventional jet fuel.

Analysts say the increase was driven by higher conventional jet fuel prices following shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as stronger demand in markets with SAF blending mandates. The UK and the European Union introduced a 2% SAF blending requirement in 2025, further supporting demand.

The most affordable SAF remains fuel produced via the HEFA pathway, averaging $1,817/t. Advanced bio-SAF made from waste feedstocks averaged $3,399/t, while synthetic e-SAF, produced from hydrogen and carbon dioxide, averaged $5,015/t—nearly seven times the price of conventional jet fuel.

Global SAF production totaled 1.9 mln tons in 2025, covering only 0.6% of worldwide jet fuel demand. This highlights a significant supply shortage as airlines continue to increase SAF consumption.

BloombergNEF expects SAF prices to continue rising in the coming years as blending mandates expand, competition for feedstocks with the road transport sector intensifies, and production capacity grows more slowly than demand.

text:
India's civil aviation regulator, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), would be preparing a mandatory carbon dioxide emissions reporting obligation for international flights, according to anonymous sources cited by Indian news agency ANI on August 4, 2026. The measure would apply to Indian and foreign airlines operating from all of the country's international airports, as part of India's preparation for the global carbon offsetting scheme for international aviation known as CORSIA (Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation), overseen by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO). The stated rationale would be to ensure equal treatment between operators and prevent an imbalance in obligations from distorting competition among carriers.

A timeline aligned with ICAO's mandatory phase

The CORSIA scheme organizes member states' participation in successive phases, before entering, for all countries exceeding a certain threshold of international traffic, its mandatory phase on a date set by ICAO. Unlike most member states, which had joined the scheme during its initial voluntary phases, India had not yet acceded to it at this stage.

Its entry into force would coincide directly with the start of the mandatory phase, a calculation that would rely notably on the weight of its past international air traffic measured in Revenue Tonne Kilometres (RTK). This direct shift would set India apart from states that had gradually ramped up within the scheme since its inception.

A sustainable fuel blending trajectory for international flights

Alongside the carbon offsetting component, the Indian government has set, in stages, a blending trajectory for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) into conventional jet fuel, applicable initially to international flights. This progression would account for the still-limited availability of domestic production capacity for this fuel, which is more expensive than conventional kerosene, and would seek to limit the pass-through of this additional cost to airlines and passengers.

The government also highlights progress made by public refineries in establishing SAF production capacity, along with the recent certification of a first domestic production site and a first dedicated certification body. These industrial milestones would directly condition the pace at which the announced blending trajectory for international flights can be applied.

Coordination between the regulator, airlines and public refiners

The Indian government says it is seeking to further involve the private sector in this capacity buildup, in a context where global supply of sustainable aviation fuel would remain considered insufficient relative to projected demand. Coordination of this roadmap was the subject of a high-level consultation between the relevant ministries, the civil aviation regulator, airlines, airport operators and public oil companies. The meeting aimed in particular to advance work on emissions accounting and verification, ahead of the country's entry into CORSIA's mandatory phase.

Revised SAF expansion plan Calumet outlined a revised approach for expanding SAF production at Montana Renewables.

About Calumet (NASDAQ:CLMT) Calumet Specialty Products Partners, L.P. NASDAQ: CLMT is an independent provider of high-value, essential product solutions derived from both petroleum and renewable feedstocks.
text:
2 Energy Stocks Surging on Billion-Dollar DOE Loan Commitments

Calumet NASDAQ: CLMT reported second-quarter adjusted EBITDA with tax attributes of $175 million, as strong performance in its Specialty Products and Solutions business helped offset downtime tied to planned turnarounds and the first phase of its MaxSAF 150 expansion at Montana Renewables.

Chief Executive Officer Todd Borgmann said the company began the period with three planned turnarounds at Princeton, Cotton Valley and Montana Renewables. Despite that activity, Calumet’s restricted-group leverage ratio fell below four times. Borgmann said the company expects to surpass three times leverage in the next quarter as cash flow supports faster debt reduction.

During the quarter and shortly afterward, Calumet called $100 million of notes and repurchased its CMR truck-rack sale-leaseback arrangement for $115 million, eliminating what Borgmann described as high-interest debt. Chief Financial Officer David Lunin said the debt reduction following the quarter was funded predominantly by cash generated from quarterly earnings.

Specialties segment drives earnings

Specialty Products and Solutions generated adjusted EBITDA of $161.7 million, more than double the prior-year figure. Lunin said the result reflected commercial and operating execution, including the full realization of more than 20 specialty-product price increases put in place during the first quarter.

The company completed planned turnarounds at Princeton and Cotton Valley on time and on budget, according to Lunin. Calumet has no turnarounds scheduled for the third quarter, while Shreveport is scheduled for a turnaround in the fourth quarter.

Specialty sales volumes exceeded 20,000 barrels per day for the seventh consecutive quarter, while specialty production reached a record during the period. Year-to-date specialty volumes were up more than 5% from 2025 levels, Lunin said.

Borgmann attributed the favorable market to global shortages in paraffinic base oils, as well as high fuel and asphalt values generated as co-products from specialty production. He said more than 10% of global paraffinic base-oil capacity was offline, with Middle Eastern capacity affected by the Iranian war and European Group I production reduced during the Russo-Ukrainian war.

Calumet produces both Group I and Group II base oils. Scott Obermeier, president of Specialties, said demand for those products has strengthened as customers seek substitutes for constrained Group III supply. He also cited refinery decisions to divert production toward distillates amid high crack spreads, along with additional refinery disruptions in Russia.

“We view the market as being tight, and we expect that to continue certainly into the coming months here through 2026,” Obermeier said.

Performance Brands recorded adjusted EBITDA of $6.3 million, down about $6.2 million from the prior year. Lunin said volume increased 18%, but higher input costs arrived before pricing actions could fully flow through to retail customers. He said the segment also faced a $7 million headwind from LIFO accounting during a period of rapid cost inflation, and management expects margins to recover as pricing catches up and inventory effects reverse.

Montana Renewables ramps after expansion downtime

Montana Renewables posted $17 million of adjusted EBITDA with tax attributes during the second quarter, although the site was offline throughout April and for part of May as it completed the first stage of the MaxSAF 150 expansion, a turnaround and recovery from a power outage. Lunin estimated that the downtime represented more than $40 million of foregone margin opportunity.

Management said the newly installed MaxSAF catalyst passed its performance test and met or exceeded expectations. The company expects third-quarter earnings at Montana Renewables to be meaningfully higher as the site operates for a full quarter and benefits from stronger renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, economics.

Lunin said renewable diesel index margins were approximately $2.60 per gallon and rising at the time of the call. Borgmann said the renewable volume obligation, or RVO, has supported a measured restart of biodiesel capacity, while soybean and canola crushing have reached record levels.

Bruce Fleming, executive vice president of Montana Renewables and corporate development, said Calumet’s view of mid-cycle renewable diesel margins has not changed. He said the market needs cash margins sufficient to cover fully loaded costs in order to bring capacity back online, and characterized 2024 as an aberration tied to the prior rulemaking.

Revised SAF expansion plan

Calumet outlined a revised approach for expanding SAF production at Montana Renewables. Rather than transporting a second reactor from the Gulf Coast as part of a larger project, the company plans to repurpose an existing reactor at its Great Falls site. Borgmann said the approach is expected to be cheaper, faster, lower risk and more capital efficient than the original plan.

The repurposed reactor will be used in a patent-pending polishing service designed to minimize lower-value byproducts, including renewable naphtha and fuel gas. Management said the configuration should improve SAF yields compared with a more severe cracking process.

Calumet expects to operate at an economically optimal SAF run rate of about 60 million gallons until a site reconfiguration planned for early winter. The company expects the reconfiguration to allow production to ramp to an 80 million to 100 million gallon annual run rate by the end of 2026 and more than 120 million gallons by spring 2027. Over the next two years, management expects the site to reach roughly 200 million gallons of SAF capacity as total fresh-feed rates rise to 17,000 barrels per day.

Borgmann said Calumet delayed the fossil-side reactor conversion because current CMR market conditions are expected to generate more than $50 million of EBITDA before the winter reconfiguration. The company plans to retain operations at CMR, including asphalt and gasoline racks, crude processing and the shared workforce supporting Montana Renewables.

Management said it expects to provide further details on the Department of Energy modification process, project costs, funding and the site reconfiguration before its next earnings call.

Capital allocation priorities

Calumet said it is examining a pipeline of low-risk, high-return specialty growth projects after directing most discretionary capital in recent years toward Montana Renewables and debt reduction. Borgmann said a number of projects could clear the front-end-loading process for deployment in 2027 and 2028.

The company discussed approximately $50 million of specialty growth capital spending, with most of the cash outlay expected in 2027 and the remainder in 2028. Management said the projects are generally smaller debottlenecking and expansion initiatives, with most financial benefits expected in 2028.

Borgmann also said Calumet continues to view a future separation or monetization of Montana Renewables as the appropriate long-term path, but said accelerated deleveraging means such a transaction is no longer required before investing in the specialties business. He said management will assess any potential Montana Renewables transaction through the lens of shareholder-value optimization while continuing to prioritize debt reduction.

About Calumet (NASDAQ:CLMT)

Calumet Specialty Products Partners, L.P. NASDAQ: CLMT is an independent provider of high-value, essential product solutions derived from both petroleum and renewable feedstocks. The company operates an integrated network of manufacturing plants, blending terminals and storage facilities across North America, delivering customized products and technical services to industrial, automotive, consumer and agricultural end markets. By leveraging its scale and technical expertise, Calumet tailors supply chain and formulation solutions to meet stringent regulatory and performance requirements.

Calumet's product portfolio includes specialty lubricants and base oils for high-performance applications; process oils and waxes for food-grade, cosmetic and packaging uses; industrial solvents and cleaning solutions; and fuel additives designed to optimize engine performance and emissions.

Management reported a reorganization of leadership across four product lines to increase execution speed and innovation. Minerals Technologies announced new 10-year environmental targets through 2035 following the completion of its previous sustainability goals. CEO Dietrich announced organizational changes that elevated four leaders to oversee product lines, stating the move will "more closely align the people, products, facilities and core technologies that serve similar markets and strengthen execution across the organization."

The company published its 18th annual sustainability report, highlighting a 40% reduction in CO2 emissions and the elimination of coal at all but one facility since 2018.

Management confirmed that three new satellite facilities for the paper and packaging business are all progressing, with another substantial Asia facility planned for early 2027.

CEO Dietrich noted that the sustainable aviation fuel order book is strong, stating the bleaching earth expansion allows the company to "begin working through a very strong order book from sustainable aviation fuel customers."

Management scheduled an Investor Day for Sept. 22 at the Bethlehem, Pennsylvania research and development facility to showcase crystal engineering and engineered blend technologies.

INDUSTRY GLOSSARY

Bentonite: An absorbent aluminum phyllosilicate clay used in cat litter, foundry molds, and environmental barriers.

EBITDA: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, used as a measure of core operating performance.

Net Leverage: A financial ratio of net debt to EBITDA used to measure a company's ability to cover its debt obligations.

PCC: Precipitated Calcium Carbonate, a synthetic mineral used as a functional filler in paper, plastics, and coatings.

PFAS: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, synthetic chemicals that require specialized remediation technologies like the company's FLUORO-SORB product.

Refractory: Heat-resistant materials used to line high-temperature furnaces, reactors, and kilns.

SAF: Sustainable Aviation Fuel, a low-carbon jet fuel alternative produced from renewable resources.

You'd want to be closer to 14% perhaps. But -- we do have that typical seasonality in Q4 and Q1 every year.

Dan Moore: Yes. Very helpful. One more, I'll jump out. Maybe just a little bit more color on sort of update on the BMI case. How did we come to the determination of the funding, the trust and the $290 million charge? And I know it's not apples-to-apples, but obviously, J&J just came to an agreement. How does that sort of impact your confidence about the ability to get this settled and put it behind you? Any commentary there would be helpful, if possible.

Douglas Dietrich: Yes. So maybe I'll answer the second part first. We saw the news on other J&Js and their settlement. That really doesn't -- it's a different torque. It doesn't have much bearing it's probably some positive news for them to get through that or at least come to some final, but that really doesn't have a bearing on ours, our cases. What I will say is, yes, we determined to increase our reserve for the potential for the funding of a potential plan that we filed to meet that core deadline.

We were in mediation for many weeks before that. we wanted to put in a plan that we felt provided finality to the company and that we felt was a fair settlement. And through that mediation in those discussions, we determined that, that was a very rich offer to be able to put that down and get finality for the company. Since then, I think you might have seen that the bankruptcy has been abated, and the gating causation issue has been moved into district court, and that's where we sit now. Right now, we're just in the scheduling.

So there's not much to talk about there, but we're in the scheduling aspects of that trial and that resolving that issue. So that's where we are. That's how we came to that determination. We wanted some finality for the company and get this behind us and we'll see where we go from here.

Operator: The next question comes from Mike Harrison with Seaport Research Partners.

Michael Harrison: Was hoping that we could get just maybe a little bit more color on what's going on in the PC and H business. Just really surprised that you guys were guiding to a high single-digit growth number, and I believe it was a 3-ish percent decline. I understand there were some pieces that didn't play out relative to your expectations. But I guess, what were some of the key drivers of that meaningful shortfall? And I guess, what gives you confidence that you're going to see momentum pick back up in Q3.

Erik Aldag: Yes, Mike, I guess, let me start just with kind of bridging the shortfall to our expectations. I mean it was really 3 things. The easing off of the cat litter orders from the strong Q1, we probably overestimated where we were going to be just based on how strong the first quarter was -- but like DJ said, I think we're pretty happy with the year-to-date 9% growth and then seeing the orders pick back up into the third quarter. No real concerns there, but it was a difference from where our expectations were. The other piece was the bleaching earth expansion.

Doug already mentioned, fully ramped up at the end of the second quarter, but we had assumed some sales in the second quarter for that expansion. The only other piece I would mention is the personal care campaign that was in the second quarter last year. We were expecting it earlier in the year this year. that's moved to the second half as well. So we had a few things shift, I would say, from the second quarter after the second half, but we're still feeling confident about the growth rates for those businesses going forward.

D. J. Monagle: Yes, Mike, I would just add to that, that -- so Erik summarize as well the -- our interpretation of what we were thinking going into the second quarter. What I'm telling you what I'm seeing as we're going into the third is pretty strong pull that supports some promotional activity with some key retailers that we've got. That is a combination of new products with them and some new SKUs of old products, repackaging of old products. And so right now, that poll looks very strong on the pet side. We got some increased momentum really across the U.S. on pet. On the Bleaching Earth, we're very bullish about that.

We -- some minor delays in getting the project up and running, but we're also impeded by some shipping challenges that were associated with some geopolitical issues. We've worked through that. We've got the strong supply chain going forward, supplying the sustainable aviation fuels that also got a good base of edible oils underneath it. So we're feeling really good about leaching earth, supporting that pet care growth. And again, the personal care item was just a shift from the second quarter into the third versus -- on that. And so that still looks like it's going to take off. So we feel very good about this quarter coming up.

Michael Harrison: All right. And while we're on the topic, I believe last quarter, you referenced a new laundry innovation or new product that a customer was going to be launching. Any update on the timing of any benefit from the laundry business.

D. J. Monagle: Yes. Thanks for the question, Mike. Glad to address that. We have done a -- the team has done a great job on our end on getting -- our portion of that lined up. It is in dry laundry. It is supporting some innovations out there in the market. So everything on our end is good. Everything is qualified. The supply chain is set and ready to go, and now we just are success will be dependent on how that new product responds in the market. So we feel good about that.

I don't know that it's so much in the third quarter as the fourth, but it's entirely dependent on the success of our partner and how the market is embracing that.

Michael Harrison: All right. And then over on the refractory side, you noted some improved pull from European steel customers. I assume that's Mican that's driving that. But I guess any additional detail on what you're seeing and whether you think that momentum could continue.

Douglas Dietrich: Go ahead, Brett.

Brett Argirakis: \ Yes, this is Brett. Mike, look, the European market is -- it's still soft, but it has improved over the prior quarter. There's been some carbon regulation safeguards that have finally been put into place, and that's really helped the threat of imports and it's improved production. We're seeing really a lot of that production in Germany that is improving. But overall, we're starting to see some improvements. The U.K. just nationalized one of their major steel mills that's going to be positive. It's been a plan that we've had business with for many, many years. So when that -- they're going to actually expand and put a third blast furnace into that production.

Of course, we're seeing some -- our Middle East business, which is part of the European growth. We're doing pretty well despite the Iran conflict, but of course, the lanes and the logistics have been -- caused a little bit of commotion. But overall, we haven't lost any business. We continue to sell and we are seeing a little bit bigger uptick in the steel production. So we -- that's a good sign. As far as the min scans in Europe, we have 4 units now outside of the U.S. and we installed 1 in Europe this year. So there's more to come when we see more opportunities in Europe as the electric furnace steel production expands.

Operator: And the next question comes from Pete Osterland with Julius Securities.

Peter Osterland: So I wanted to start just by digging in a little more specifically on the CNS margins. You mentioned that higher costs haven't yet been fully recovered due to some contractual timing. What percentage of your sales within CNS are still awaiting contract resets? I guess right way to think about it? And should we be thinking about maybe a 200 basis point or higher margin snapback specifically in the third quarter? Or will this more likely be a multi-quarter recovery trajectory?

Erik Aldag: Yes. Pete, this is Eric. Thanks for the question. So look, yes, in terms of getting the consumer and Specialties margins back to target, the biggest thing right now is the price cost catch up. And the fact that costs are continuing to rise, means that, that's going to be pushed out to the fourth quarter. So we're not expecting a major improvement Q2 to Q3. I would say the other things we have going for us longer term is just the growth of higher margin these consumer specialties that we talk about, that's going to help the mix overall. And just higher volumes in general just will help with fixed cost leverage.

But in terms of your specific questions around the percent of contracts with a delay, a lot of that sits in the household and personal care product line within Consumer and Specialties. Historically, we've had more of a pricing lag within Specialty Additives, for example, in the paper and packaging business. We've done a lot of work there in terms of tightening up those legs and less so of an impact these days in that product line.

Peter Osterland: Got it. Very helpful. And then also just on the record margins within Engineered Solutions. Was there any degree of the second quarter margin performance that you view as overearning as opposed to permanent operational efficiency improvements. I guess, is it fair for us to be thinking about 17% plus is the structural floor for the segment going forward?

Erik Aldag: Yes. Those margins are solid. The segment is performing very well. I wouldn't call anything out of special or unusual for the second quarter. I would say, if you're looking sequentially Q2 to Q3, you do have some typical seasonality in terms of customer and maintenance shutdowns in Europe for some of the more industrial businesses. But I think we're setting a new baseline for this business from a margin perspective.

Douglas Dietrich: Yes. And Peter, I think the only thing I'd add to that is we kind of signaled that there was some pent-up profitability in this business, right? So the high temperature Technologies business, operating really well, new products, midscans, contractual volumes coming through. Steel markets are in Europe are improving. North America has been strong for the past year or so. But we've had almost 2 years of kind of a lull in our Environmental Products business, and that's starting to turn a little bit. We've had 5 quarters of growth in that business in that product line.

And we said as that starts to turn, that's a lot of contribution that comes through its project-based, a little bit lumpy still. But at the same time, we're starting to see our offshore oil grew 22% in the first half of the year. Drilling products and infrastructure for infrastructure drilling has been really doing well. Building products is starting to turn in our environmental products and water products and Fluororb is in there, too. So we still see there's more growth potential. So that business, as you start to see these volumes of 1 of these product lines start to move really drops to the bottom line and good contribution, and that's what you're seeing. We think that's stable.

Now the other side of the business, still good growth, right? We've got, as Erik mentioned, that lag that we're going to move ourselves through and those costs park there, a lot of transportation, energy, we'll get that pushed through, but that growth is there, and we start to leverage that growth to the bottom line. I think that's a -- yes, we've got some work to do in the household and personal care business and cost. But once we get that work done, I think we got to both sides of the business kind of moving along. That's where we see that margin improvement.

With the 17 on 1 side and moving the other side up to 14, you start to start to see that 15%, 16% as we push through. Now a lot of things have to line up. It's got some work to do, but I think we're setting up for that margin improvement. It's unfortunate we have this delay still, but we'll move through it and we'll deliver that profitability.

Operator: The next question comes from David Silver with Freedom Capital Markets.

David Silver: A little trouble joining the call at the beginning, so apologies if I make you repeat yourself. I wanted to drill down, I guess, with DJ on a couple of the expansion projects that are underway. And in particular, I guess, there was a series of PCC satellites that were due to turn on this year. Just wondering where we are on that and what the contribution might have been in the second quarter? And then just on the edible oil, you did explain the timing. It's complete. The order book is full, but revenues will probably start in the third quarter.

With the full order book and the project complete, I'm just wondering about next steps there, like what might be the cadence for the next incremental expansion, assuming the SAF market continues to progress, which I think is a pretty sure thing myself personally. And then is the expansion program, 1 where the incremental additions are more of a modular nature. In other words, they can be added relatively quickly? Or is this more of a discrete project with its own separate, I don't know, off-sites or supporting utilities? Just what might be the cadence that we should think about for growth in your capacity on the edible oil side, edible oil purification side?

D. J. Monagle: So David, I'm going to try and unpack that a little bit. Let me let me deal with the first part of the question on the PCC. I would say, as Erik had indicated and Doug had indicated, all 3 of those are up, running, contributed in the second quarter, and they'll they look like they're going to be a good business for us moving forward. There's another 1 that we have mentioned in the past, it comes online in -- so we're building another satellite right now. It's a pretty substantial satellite that supports packaging growth in Asia.

And so that's -- so we had the 3 that came up running in the second quarter contributing in the second quarter and another one still to come that will be early in '27. So paper is looking solid. And then I would say that the nature of that pipeline still remains healthy. 20-plus projects in the pipeline, a blend of packaging and new yield and PCC and the new products we've introduced. So we feel pretty good on that side of things. Shifting gears now to the question. So we just put in that expansion.

It's reasonable for you to think of that 1 as a modular expansion, pretty efficient in getting it up and running and designing the products specifically for these customers getting them qualified with the customer. And so we're up and running, and that will be -- you'll start seeing that pretty much running full out in this third quarter. We are looking further at expansions. The next one probably is a bigger magnitude one, but we still got to line up some volumes on that.

I would tell you, though, that from what we've been able to do with both the quality of the ore and the reserves that we've got, especially in Turkey, plus the scientists that we've got working at Hoffman states. We feel very good about that product line and what it's able to contribute differently in the market, especially in sustainable aviation fuel. So we're happy with this last expansion. We are happy with the qualifications that we've been able to do and the pace in which we've been able to bring them in and we'll get ready to expand further, but nothing to announce on that just yet.

David Silver: Okay. Great. And I hope you'll indulge me here, but I wanted to go back to the $290 million charge that was taken. And I just want to make sure I have things lined up. But back in -- so there's a total funding of the 524G trust of $450 million. And I believe in first quarter of 2025, you allocated, I believe, 185 of your total charge then for the trust. Is it correct to say that of the $290 million, I guess, the 265 were the balance to get to 450.

So $265 million of the $290 million goes to the trust and the balance of $25 million or so is for estimated other costs -- is that correct? Or...

Erik Aldag: Dave, this is Erik. So you're close. There's a portion in there that's to fund the ongoing process. And so right now, there's about $450 million in terms of potential 529G funding and about $35 million in terms of ongoing process funding. And that's made up of the charge we just took and the one from 2025.

David Silver: Okay. Great. And then I don't know if you can answer this or not, but -- so you have set up a trust that you believe is acceptable to settle all the ultimate claims. However, the bankruptcy judge as you pointed out, has abated his process in favor of letting the District Court work on the issue of causation. Doug, I guess this is how determined or how do you feel about letting that district court process run its course versus maybe pursuing something sooner, but that may ultimately prove to be a little more expensive for your company.

How do you kind of weigh the pros and cons of settling sooner versus letting the district court process or on its course?

Douglas Dietrich: Yes, David, I'm not going to answer that question. I don't -- we're right in the midst of the beginning of litigation. And so I don't want to speculate on outcomes in district courts or the ramifications of that right now. I think where we are is we filed a plan that we feel is there and provides finality to the company -- for the company. We've always maintained that as Minerals BMI Old [indiscernible] has been safe. And so the District Court taking on that issue, we see that as a positive because we've always maintained this to be the case.

But we're right in the beginning of that, and we're going to be going through the process of scheduling and seeing how that goes. And I just don't want to speculate on where we land at the moment right now, given where we are.

David Silver: Fair enough. I appreciate that. And then last thing for me. I did just want to get a PFAS update. I believe last quarter, -- the plan was to have 10 commercial projects start up through 2026. And then I am curious, but I did watch the EPA panel discussion where your company was 1 of just a hand full featured. And I'm just wondering if that presentation and that opportunity for interested parties has resulted in an acceleration of trial and beta testing. So just an update on progress with commercializing PFAS and then your take on what has happened since the -- your participation in the EPA panel?

Brett Argirakis: David, it's Brett. Let me just give you a quick update on where we stand with FLUORO-SORB and hopefully, I can answer your questions. FLUORO-SORB are really, it continues to gain traction. And we do have the 10 full-scale municipal drinking water plants up and running. The good news is we now have 18 municipal systems specified for upcoming installations. Most of those will start. They're all -- most of them are under construction. Several of them will start in '26 and others will start in '27. So in that, we're gaining traction. We also expect to see more of the pilot projects for the small groundwater treatment plants move into full scale.

So a lot of that will start to move over the next several months. We do -- as you know, we also use the FLUORO-SORB in-situ remediation and we're working with the Department of War and other aviation-related fields based on the success we've seen with the Department of War, we're expanding that project. And we have -- actually, we have 2 big projects that will happen in the third quarter and both our airports and one is a military site. So that is working. And it's really based on the absorption technology of the FLUORO-SORB. So it's working very well. The other update I'll give you is we also continue our discussions with the U.S.

EPA Office of Water and Office of and emergency management. Both are really committed to the PFAS remediation and disposal research. So we're working with them to wrap this up and the Croda agreement. And I think once that is finalized, then the research will expand much more rapidly. But it's Things are moving well, and we expect to see additional municipalities taking on the floors here.

Operator: This concludes our question-and-answer session. I would like to turn the conference back over to Doug Dietrich for any closing remarks.

Douglas Dietrich: Thank you, Dave. Appreciate it. I appreciate everyone joining the call today. If you have any follow-up questions, happy to answer them after the call, but we'll talk to you in about 3 months. Thank you.

title: SAF Production Facilities - Clean the Sky
description:
SkyNRG and KLM began construction on 'DSL-01,' the Netherlands' first facility dedicated to producing sustainable aviation fuel, marking the first commercial-scale SAF plant globally to secure non-recourse project financing.
KLM serves as the primary off-taker for the fuel produced, with its long-term offtake commitment playing a key role in enabling the project's financing.
Once operational in 2028, the Delfzijl facility is expected to produce approximately 100,000 tonnes of SAF annually from low-quality feedstocks such as used cooking oil, processed through the HEFA pathway to deliver significantly lower lifecycle emissions than conventional jet fuel.
The project received a €16 million subsidy from the European Just Transition Fund, supporting Northern Netherlands' shift away from its historically gas-dependent economy while creating more than 100 direct jobs.
