title: Building the market behind Sustainable Aviation Fuel - LinkedIn
description:
Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is widely regarded as aviation’s most promising pathway to reducing emissions.
Creating a fuel market, not just fuel Scaling Sustainable Aviation Fuel appears to be a production challenge, centred on refinery capacity, feedstock and output.
Airbus has invested in LanzaJet to accelerate Alcohol-to-Jet (ATJ) technology and expand commercial SAF production, while also backing the Sustainable Aviation Fuel Financing Alliance (SAFFA) to improve access to capital for new projects.
Airbus is also the anchor investor in the Sustainable Aviation Fuel Financing Alliance, whose founding partners committed approximately US$200 million.
The next phase of aviation competitiveness will not be determined solely by who produces the most Sustainable Aviation Fuel.
text:
Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is widely regarded as aviation’s most promising pathway to reducing emissions. Yet producing the fuel is only one part of the challenge. Scaling SAF depends on building a commercially viable market where refiners, airlines, airports, investors and policymakers can invest with confidence. Production capacity alone cannot create that market. As governments introduce blending mandates and companies expand production, the next phase of aviation competitiveness will increasingly depend on how effectively countries build the commercial ecosystem that enables SAF to scale.

Creating a fuel market, not just fuel

Scaling Sustainable Aviation Fuel appears to be a production challenge, centred on refinery capacity, feedstock and output. Yet recent investments suggest otherwise. A commercially viable SAF market depends on coordinated investment across the value chain, where producers, airlines, airports, investors and policymakers have enough certainty to commit capital before supply and demand fully mature. Refiners require long-term demand visibility before financing new production facilities, while airlines remain cautious about committing to long-term purchases until supply expands and prices become more competitive. Airports, lenders and investors face similar decisions over infrastructure and project viability. This coordination gap can delay projects even where technology and feedstock are available.

Global markets are increasingly addressing this challenge through collaborative investment models. Neste began SAF production at its modified Rotterdam refinery in April 2025, increasing its global SAF production capability to 1.5 million tonnes annually. Airbus has invested in LanzaJet to accelerate Alcohol-to-Jet (ATJ) technology and expand commercial SAF production, while also backing the Sustainable Aviation Fuel Financing Alliance (SAFFA) to improve access to capital for new projects. Meanwhile, TotalEnergies has expanded its collaboration with Airbus, supplying more than half of the manufacturer’s European SAF requirements while supporting broader efforts to stimulate demand and production capacity.

India is beginning to build similar foundations. Indian Oil is developing SAF production from used cooking oil at its Panipat refinery, while Bharat Petroleum is commissioning a co-processing unit at its Mumbai refinery. India has set indicative SAF blending targets for international flights of 1% by 2027, 2% by 2028 and 5% by 2030. The targets are not yet binding, but they provide an early demand signal for producers and airlines. Together, these developments signal the early stages of a coordinated SAF market.

When coordination becomes an investment strategy

Increasingly, investment decisions extend beyond traditional buyer-supplier relationships, recognising that no single participant can scale the market independently. In July 2026, Bharat Petroleum and Akasa Air signed an agreement to develop a framework for supplying SAF-blended aviation fuel, including sharing demand forecasts to improve production planning. Shared demand planning reduces commercial uncertainty for both companies by improving demand visibility. It enables producers to plan capacity expansion with greater confidence while giving airlines stronger assurance over future fuel availability, reducing the investment risks associated with scaling SAF production. A similar pattern is emerging globally. Delta Air Lines and Shell recently expanded their collaboration through a five-year agreement to increase SAF supply and supporting infrastructure across major airport hubs. Much like Power Purchase Agreements accelerated renewable energy deployment by guaranteeing future electricity demand, long-term SAF offtake agreements can improve project bankability, strengthen access to financing and support investment in additional capacity.

Airbus and Cathay Group have separately committed up to US$70 million to identify, evaluate and invest in SAF projects in Asia and globally. Airbus is also the anchor investor in the Sustainable Aviation Fuel Financing Alliance, whose founding partners committed approximately US$200 million. Together with investments in financing and infrastructure, these collaborations demonstrate that capital is increasingly flowing into the market structures needed to make SAF commercially scalable. A World Economic Forum and Kearney study estimates that meeting projected global SAF demand of 17 million tonnes annually by 2030 could require between US$19 billion and US$45 billion in capital expenditure.

What India is really competing for

India’s opportunity extends well beyond achieving future blending targets. India is expected to handle around 500 million passengers annually by 2030, reinforcing its position as one of the world’s fastest-growing aviation markets. Combined with extensive refining capacity, abundant agricultural residue and an established biofuels ecosystem built through its ethanol blending programme, these advantages position India to compete in a market that is still taking shape globally. Realising that opportunity, however, will depend on investment, infrastructure and demand expanding alongside production.

Other markets are pursuing the same objective through different policy and commercial mechanisms. Singapore has deferred the introduction of its Sustainable Aviation Fuel levy, which will now apply to tickets and services sold from October 2026 for flights departing from January 2027, to strengthen demand certainty, while the European Union’s ReFuelEU Aviation regulation establishes progressively increasing SAF blending mandates to stimulate long-term investment across the supply chain. SAF remains significantly more expensive than conventional jet fuel, while feedstocks compete with other industries. Certification requirements, financing risks and consistent policy support continue to constrain commercial deployment.

The global market reflects the same reality. Worldwide SAF production reached approximately 1.9 million tonnes in 2025, falling short of earlier industry expectations despite growing policy support. Global SAF production reached approximately 1.9 million tonnes in 2025, equivalent to only 0.6% of worldwide jet fuel consumption, according to IATA. Separate government and industry estimates place India’s potential SAF output at approximately 19 to 24 million tonnes annually, although converting that theoretical potential into commercial supply will depend on feedstock mobilisation, technology maturity, certification and project economics.

Investing before demand peaks

India’s SAF ambitions are beginning to attract investment across production, infrastructure and demand. Whether those commitments translate into long-term competitiveness will depend on sustained policy support, commercial partnerships and private capital. As demand accelerates, countries that reduce uncertainty across producers, airlines, financiers and infrastructure providers will be better positioned to attract investment and scale production.

The next phase of aviation competitiveness will not be determined solely by who produces the most Sustainable Aviation Fuel. It will be shaped by which markets create the strongest conditions for investment around it. Countries that provide credible demand signals, stable policy frameworks and coordinated infrastructure will be better positioned to attract capital early, strengthen domestic supply chains and influence the future economics of sustainable aviation.

title: Infinium's Waste-CO2 Jet Fuel Enters US Commercial Airport Tanks for First Time
description:
American Airlines and Infinium described the flight as the first delivery of sustainable aviation fuel made without biobased feedstocks to a commercial airport in the United States.
Infinium states its eSAF can reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by over 90% compared to conventional petroleum-based jet fuel.
Infinium blended its eSAF batch with conventional jet fuel at the Pathfinder facility and tested the blended product against the ASTM aviation fuel standard for Jet A — the universal standard that every drop of commercial aviation fuel must meet before it enters an aircraft.
Infinium's eSAF batch was blended with conventional Jet A and tested to meet the ASTM International specification for aviation turbine fuel (Jet A), the same standard all commercial aviation fuel must meet.
Fischer-Tropsch fuel is also zero-sulfur, which means it produces lower particulate emissions and may reduce contrail formation compared to conventional kerosene.
text:
A scheduled American Airlines passenger flight from Corpus Christi to Dallas–Fort Worth has cleared the barrier that clean-aviation skeptics said mattered most: a synthetic jet fuel made entirely from captured carbon dioxide and renewable electricity moved through a conventional commercial airport's shared fuel system and into an aircraft without a single modification to the plane, the fuel trucks, or the storage infrastructure. American Airlines and Infinium announced the milestone on August 6, 2026.

The flight departed Corpus Christi International Airport (CRP) and landed at Dallas–Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) on August 6, 2026, operating on electro sustainable aviation fuel (eSAF) produced by clean-fuels startup Infinium at its Pathfinder facility — the first commercial-scale power-to-liquids plant in the world, operating in Corpus Christi since 2023. According to Aviation Week's eSAF delivery report, the aircraft was an Embraer E175 regional jet.

American Airlines and Infinium described the flight as the first delivery of sustainable aviation fuel made without biobased feedstocks to a commercial airport in the United States. To the passengers on board, it was unremarkable. That is the point.

How Waste Carbon Becomes Jet Fuel: A Century-Old Chemistry Finally Doing Its Intended Job

To understand why this flight is significant, it helps to know that the chemical process at its heart is not new. The Fischer-Tropsch synthesis — the catalytic reaction that converts a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen gas into liquid hydrocarbons — was first reported by chemists Franz Fischer and Hans Tropsch in 1926, exactly 100 years ago. Nature's centennial Fischer-Tropsch review confirms that Germany built nine Fischer-Tropsch plants by the end of World War II, pursuing petroleum independence through synthetic fuel. The goal then was the same as the goal now: make liquid fuel without petroleum. The chemistry solved that problem a century ago. The barriers since have been cost and scale, not knowledge.

Infinium's process at Pathfinder runs the synthesis with a different carbon source and a different energy input than the wartime version, but the underlying logic is identical. Renewable electricity drives electrolyzers that split water molecules into green hydrogen and oxygen. That hydrogen is combined with waste carbon dioxide — captured from industrial exhaust streams that would otherwise vent into the atmosphere — through Infinium's proprietary eSAF process at Pathfinder, which uses a reverse water-gas shift (RWGS) catalyst to produce syngas: a mixture of hydrogen and carbon monoxide. The syngas is then fed through a Fischer-Tropsch reactor, where a catalyst drives the assembly of long-chain liquid hydrocarbons.

The result is chemically identical to petroleum-derived jet fuel. It contains no sulfur — Fischer-Tropsch output measures below one ppm sulfur typically, compared to the sulfur present in conventional kerosene — and it produces no direct process emissions during manufacturing. Unlike most sustainable aviation fuel on the market today, which is made from used cooking oil, animal fats, or agricultural residues, Infinium's eSAF requires no biomass whatsoever. That sidesteps the feedstock constraints — land use, food competition, supply limits — that researchers expect will cap the growth of biofuel-based SAF after 2030, according to the ICCT analysis of SAF barriers.

The eSAF batch used for the August 6 flight carries ISCC PLUS certification from the International Sustainability and Carbon Certification organization. Infinium states its eSAF can reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by over 90% compared to conventional petroleum-based jet fuel.

What Does It Mean to Clear the 'Common Tank'?

Producing a certified fuel is only half the challenge. The harder question for power-to-liquids technology has been supply-chain integration: can an eSAF batch move through the same pipes, tanks, and fueling trucks that every other airline at a given airport uses — without segregated handling, dedicated infrastructure, or special modification?

Infinium blended its eSAF batch with conventional jet fuel at the Pathfinder facility and tested the blended product against the ASTM aviation fuel standard for Jet A — the universal standard that every drop of commercial aviation fuel must meet before it enters an aircraft. Under ASTM's framework for approved synthetic aviation fuel pathways, the D7566 specification for synthetic fuels allows synthetic components to comprise up to 50% of a final blend; once blended to meet the Jet A specification, the fuel is treated as standard Jet A with no further restrictions.

The certified blend was then delivered to the common jet fuel tanks at Corpus Christi International Airport — the shared storage infrastructure through which all carriers at the airport draw their fuel — and allocated to the American Airlines E175 bound for Dallas–Fort Worth. No aircraft modifications. No specialized fueling equipment. No segregated handling.

This "common tank" delivery distinguishes the Corpus Christi flight from earlier SAF demonstrations, some of which used dedicated or segregated fuel handling. By entering and exiting the standard shared infrastructure without incident, Infinium's eSAF demonstrated that it can integrate into existing aviation supply chains — a prerequisite for any fuel that wants to scale beyond demonstration flights.

What the Aviation Sector Is Up Against

The flight's significance reads differently once you set it against the scale of the problem. Global aviation consumes nearly 100 billion gallons of conventional jet fuel every year and carries more than 4 billion passengers annually. Sustainable aviation fuel — all types combined, including biofuels — accounted for approximately 0.7% of global jet fuel consumption in 2025, growing to a projected 0.8% in 2026, according to the IATA SAF statistics page. The aviation sector's own stated goal of net-zero emissions by 2050 would require SAF production to expand to roughly 500 million tonnes annually — more than 250 times current production levels.

Power-to-liquids eSAF is a particularly nascent sub-category within that already-tiny market. The EU's ReFuelEU Aviation eSAF mandate has set a dedicated eSAF sub-mandate starting at 0.7% of total fuel supplied by 2030, specifically because regulators recognize that this pathway needs deliberate policy support to reach commercial scale.

Against that backdrop, the Corpus Christi flight is not a solution. It is a proof-of-concept for one critical part of the path to a solution: the demonstration that biofeedstock-free synthetic fuel can enter and exit the real-world airport fuel infrastructure that any solution must ultimately use.

Project Roadrunner: The Next Step

Pathfinder was always designed as a proof-of-concept facility. Infinium's commercial ambitions center on its next project: Roadrunner, currently under construction in Reeves County, Texas, near the city of Pecos, in the Permian Basin — a region better known for oil extraction than electrofuel production.

Roadrunner is designed to produce approximately 23,000 tonnes of eSAF and other eFuel products annually — approximately 7.6 million gallons — using renewable electricity and captured CO2, with dedicated wind-generation capacity from a subsidiary of NextEra Energy Resources. According to the Infinium Roadrunner construction announcement, the facility is expected to begin eSAF production and deliveries in 2027.

The project is backed by Brookfield Asset Management and Breakthrough Energy Catalyst, the clean-energy vehicle backed by Bill Gates and other major donors, with nonrecourse project debt from HSBC. Long-term offtake agreements are in place with both American Airlines and the International Airlines Group (IAG) — parent company of British Airways, Aer Lingus, Iberia, and Vueling — providing the commercial anchor the project requires to attract institutional capital.

American Airlines separately holds an arrangement with Citi that ties eSAF purchases from Roadrunner to Scope 3 emissions reductions from Citi employee business travel, an early example of financial institutions using aviation fuel procurement as a decarbonization lever.

At full capacity, Roadrunner's total eSAF output would represent roughly 0.0076% of global annual aviation fuel demand. The numbers remain humbling. But the same arithmetic defined the first commercial solar installations and the first offshore wind farms — industries that now supply meaningful portions of national electricity grids. The learning-curve economics are the same: each facility built at scale reduces costs for the next.

Why This Happened in South Texas

There is a geographic logic to a decarbonization breakthrough taking shape in Corpus Christi and the Permian Basin. The Corpus Christi area hosts some of the United States' largest petroleum refining capacity; the Permian Basin has been the center of the fracking revolution that made the US the world's largest oil producer. The infrastructure, the engineering workforce, and the industrial culture that built those industries now have a new application.

Congressman Vicente Gonzalez, who earned a bachelor's degree in business aviation from Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University before his legal and political career, represents Texas's 34th Congressional District, which includes Corpus Christi. He framed the announcement in energy-security terms. "South Texas has long been an energy leader, and today's sustainable aviation fuel announcement shows how our region continues to innovate," Gonzalez said on the Gonzalez official House website. "The work Infinium and American are doing in Corpus Christi strengthens our local economy while advancing our nation's energy security."

What Needs to Change Now

The technology milestone is real. The remaining barriers are economic and political, not chemical. Power-to-liquids fuel currently costs substantially more than conventional jet fuel — cost is the dominant reason eSAF remains a fraction of a fraction of global aviation fuel supply — and closing that gap requires both continued engineering learning and policy support that makes the investment economics work for project developers.

American CEO Robert Isom named the priority directly: "Scaling SAF production at lower prices is essential to reducing emissions, strengthening our long-term competitiveness, and continuing to deliver the connectivity and economic benefits that our customers rely on."

The Corpus Christi flight answers the supply-chain skeptics. Whether the economics, the policy environment, and the pace of renewable energy buildout can now conspire to scale the technology fast enough is the question that will define the next decade of aviation. Franz Fischer and Hans Tropsch solved the chemistry a century ago. The rest is left to the rest of us.

Frequently Asked Questions

What makes electrofuel different from other sustainable aviation fuels like HEFA-based SAF?

Most sustainable aviation fuel currently on the market is made from biological feedstocks — used cooking oil, animal fats, and agricultural residues — through a process called Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA). Electrofuel, or eSAF, is produced entirely from non-biological inputs: captured waste carbon dioxide, water, and renewable electricity. The synthesis process — electrolysis to produce green hydrogen, then Fischer-Tropsch chemistry to build liquid hydrocarbons — requires no biomass at all. That distinction matters because analysts project that feedstock availability will limit how much HEFA-based SAF can be produced after 2030, when aviation's SAF demand will exceed the supply of available waste oils. Electrofuel avoids that ceiling entirely. It also carries no land-use or food-competition concerns. The tradeoff is cost: power-to-liquids eSAF is currently more expensive to produce than HEFA-based fuel, which is why facilities like Infinium's Roadrunner require institutional investment and offtake agreements to be economically viable. The ICCT analysis of SAF barriers documents these dynamics in detail.

Can this fuel be used in existing aircraft without any engine modifications?

Yes — that is the specific property confirmed by the August 6 flight. Infinium's eSAF batch was blended with conventional Jet A and tested to meet the ASTM International specification for aviation turbine fuel (Jet A), the same standard all commercial aviation fuel must meet. Once a blended SAF product clears that specification, it is classified as standard Jet A and requires no modifications to aircraft engines, seals, fuel systems, or airport fueling infrastructure. The term for this is "drop-in" compatibility. The common-tank delivery at Corpus Christi International Airport — where the eSAF entered the same shared fuel storage all carriers use — demonstrated that drop-in compatibility holds not just for the aircraft but for the full airport supply chain. For technical detail on the certification pathway, see the D7566 specification for synthetic fuels.

How does the Fischer-Tropsch process that Infinium uses relate to the synthetic fuels Germany produced in World War II?

The chemistry is directly descended from the same process. Franz Fischer and Hans Tropsch developed the Fischer-Tropsch synthesis in 1926 — this year is its centennial — at the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Coal Research in Germany. Germany built nine Fischer-Tropsch plants by the end of World War II, using the process to convert coal into liquid fuel to reduce petroleum dependency. The process converts a syngas mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen into long-chain liquid hydrocarbons; the specific inputs and energy sources are different today, but the catalytic mechanism is the same. Infinium's version uses renewable electricity and captured CO2 as inputs rather than coal, which makes the fuel's lifecycle carbon footprint dramatically lower. Fischer-Tropsch fuel is also zero-sulfur, which means it produces lower particulate emissions and may reduce contrail formation compared to conventional kerosene. The Nature centennial Fischer-Tropsch review covers the full 100-year history of the process and its renewed relevance to sustainable aviation.

When will Infinium's larger Roadrunner facility be producing eSAF, and how much will it make?

Project Roadrunner is currently under construction in Reeves County, Texas, near Pecos, and is expected to begin commercial eSAF production and deliveries in 2027. At full capacity, the facility is designed to produce approximately 23,000 tonnes — around 7.6 million gallons — of eSAF and other eFuel products annually, powered by dedicated wind energy from a NextEra Energy Resources subsidiary. American Airlines holds a 10-year offtake agreement for commercial volumes of eSAF from Roadrunner, with International Airlines Group (parent of British Airways and Aer Lingus) also holding a supply agreement. For context, global aviation currently consumes roughly 100 billion gallons of jet fuel per year — so Roadrunner at full capacity would supply approximately 0.0076% of that demand, a figure that illustrates both how early this industry is and how large the eventual production ramp-up must be.

text:
Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) currently represents less than 1% of the approximately 100 billion gallons of jet fuel consumed annually by the global aviation industry. In a recent landmark achievement, American Airlines and Infinium successfully powered a commercial passenger flight using electro sustainable aviation fuel (eSAF). The flight, covering 391 miles from Corpus Christi to Dallas, signifies a notable advancement in the sector’s ongoing efforts to reduce carbon emissions.

Innovation in Fuel Production and Application

Unlike conventional jet fuel or bio-based alternatives, eSAF is synthesized from waste carbon dioxide and renewable electricity. At Infinium’s Texas facility, the eSAF was blended with traditional jet fuel to comply with existing engine specifications, enabling aircraft operation without any modifications. Infinium asserts that this fuel can reduce greenhouse gas emissions by more than 90% over its lifecycle compared to standard jet fuel.

Robert Schuetzle, CEO of Infinium, highlighted the company’s progress: “Since 2023, we have been producing scalable, drop-in eDiesel and eNaphtha at our Pathfinder facility from waste carbon and renewable energy for use in commercial trucks and plastics processing. Adding eSAF to our product slate — and seeing it power a commercial passenger flight — marks another meaningful step forward in bringing practical, low-carbon fuel solutions to industry.”

American Airlines CEO Robert Isom underscored the broader implications of the flight, stating, “Through our partnership with Infinium, we’re demonstrating how next generation technologies like eSAF can move from early investment to real-world application. Scaling SAF production at lower prices is essential to reducing emissions, strengthening our long-term competitiveness, and continuing to deliver the connectivity and economic benefits that our customers rely on.”

Challenges and Market Dynamics

Despite these technological advances, the widespread adoption of SAF faces significant obstacles. Limited production capacity and high costs remain major barriers, while regulatory uncertainty complicates long-term strategic planning. Recent policy developments, such as the European Commission’s expansion of its emissions trading system, have made airlines cautious about committing to long-term SAF purchase agreements. In contrast, some industry players, including International Airlines Group (IAG), are proactively securing long-term SAF supply contracts and investing in funds aimed at accelerating SAF development.

The rising demand for SAF is also influencing global markets. European airlines have tripled their SAF usage to comply with EU blending mandates, contributing to increased U.S. soybean oil prices and prompting producers to rely more heavily on domestic feedstocks. These shifts are reshaping the competitive landscape for both SAF producers and airlines.

Looking forward, Infinium is developing a new facility, Project Roadrunner, slated to open in 2027, which is expected to produce over 5 million gallons of eSAF annually. As the aviation industry pursues ambitious net-zero targets by 2050, scaling SAF production and addressing economic and regulatory challenges will be crucial to achieving substantial emissions reductions.

text:
On August 6, 2026, at the Dung Quat Refinery, Petrovietnam Refining and Petrochemical Corporation (BSR) officially shipped its first batch of B5 biodiesel (DO B5) produced at the refinery to two customers: Military Petroleum General Company One Member Limited Liability Company and Nam Phuc Investment Joint Stock Company.

The shipment marks an important milestone in BSR’s journey to research, develop and commercialize biofuel products, contributing to the energy transition and the development of greener, more environmentally friendly fuels in line with the Government’s and Petrovietnam’s strategic directions.

The successful commercialization of DO B5 not only demonstrates BSR’s research and production capabilities, but also reflects its commitment to supporting Vietnam’s national goals of reducing greenhouse gas emissions, increasing the use of renewable fuels and strengthening national energy security.

BSR supplied 25 m³ of B5 biodiesel to Military Petroleum General Company One Member Limited Liability Company and 19.5 m³ to Nam Phuc Investment Joint Stock Company under FCA Dung Quat delivery terms. The products were delivered from August 5 to 10, 2026, meeting BSR’s TCCS 25:2026/BSR internal standard for B5 diesel fuel, as well as other commercial terms applied in accordance with the 2026 sales contracts.

Before shipment, BSR carried out strict controls throughout the blending and quality assurance process. After blending was completed, samples were taken from all product storage tanks and tested at BSR’s laboratory to verify compliance with all required quality specifications. At the same time, relevant units collected samples for conformity assessment under Method 7 to obtain the Certificate of Conformity, ensuring that the product fully met technical requirements before being released to the market.

The first commercial batch was made possible through extensive research and careful preparation by BSR. Under a scientific and technological cooperation program between BSR and KEYLAB, the partner supplied 3,000 liters of B100 biodiesel for research and testing in the production of B5 and B10 fuels.

Following the research and testing phase, approximately 2,250 liters of B100 remained, enough to produce around 43–45 m³ of B5 biodiesel. Based on this available feedstock, BSR completed preparations for the raw materials, blending process, quality control system and other technical requirements needed to conduct the trial commercialization of the product at the Dung Quat Refinery.

Alongside the technical preparations, BSR proactively engaged with potential customers, introduced the product and agreed on a trial consumption plan. Military Petroleum General Company One Member Limited Liability Company and Nam Phuc Investment Joint Stock Company agreed to participate in the program, providing an opportunity for BSR to comprehensively evaluate the blending, shipment, transportation and actual use of the product under real-world conditions.

According to BSR, the trial production and sale of B5 biodiesel is aligned with the amount of B100 currently available. More importantly, it provides valuable technical and commercial data, as well as feedback from customers. These results will serve as a basis for BSR to further improve its production and quality control processes, refine its commercial operations and expand the market for biofuel products in the future.

B100 is pure biodiesel made entirely from Fatty Acid Methyl Ester (FAME), without any petroleum blending. The use of biofuels can help reduce greenhouse gas emissions and fine particulate matter, while replacing part of the conventional fossil fuel supply.

As a leading company in Vietnam’s refining and petrochemical industry, BSR is gradually implementing its development strategy toward a greener, more sustainable business model in response to global energy transition trends. In recent years, in addition to operating the Dung Quat Refinery at optimal capacity, BSR has continuously researched and developed new, higher-value and more environmentally friendly products, including Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), E10 RON 95 bio-gasoline and now B5 biodiesel.

The successive introduction of biofuel products to the market demonstrates BSR’s research capabilities, technological expertise and ability to respond quickly to the growing demand for cleaner energy. This is not only a significant step forward in the Corporation’s production and business activities, but also contributes to Vietnam’s commitments to reducing emissions, promoting a green and circular economy, and strengthening national energy security in the new era.
